text: Day one at the agency. The creative director hands you a pass, noise-cancelling headphones and says: “Pitch in an hour, you’re on the team.” You haven’t seen the brief yet.
left: Skim the brief in the elevator
right: Ask for an hour to get up to speed

text: 7:40 a.m. The client texts: “Looked at the layout over breakfast. Can the logo be bigger? Like three times bigger?” The logo already takes up a third of the banner.
right: Suggest a call and make the case

text: The account manager catches you at the coffee machine: “The client wants the layout to ‘breathe more.’ I promised it by lunch.” Nobody knows what “breathe” means.
right: Send the account guy to clarify

text: The office corgi has fallen asleep on your drawing tablet. The storyboard is due in three hours, and waking the corgi is considered bad form here.
left: Work with a mouse beside him

text: The designer shows up with dark circles: “I spent until 4 a.m. moving the logo two pixels left. Then back.” He asks you to take a fresh look.
left: Look and give an honest take
right: Send him home to sleep till noon

text: The intern bursts in with an idea for the yogurt campaign: “What if the yogurt is an astronaut?” The client presentation is in half an hour, and there are no other ideas.
The producer calls from the set at 6:50: it’s raining, and the script is all about a “sunny morning in the park.” The crew is already there, and every hour is paid for.
right: Wait for the weather to clear

text: The copywriter sent forty slogan options for a dry-cleaning chain. Your favorite: “We’ll even clean up your past.” The client asked for “no humor.”
Your morning inbox has 63 emails titled “Edits.” All from one client, all sent overnight, some contradicting each other. Where to start?
left: Read them in order from the first

text: The art director wants the font changed across the whole campaign: “This font is shouting, we need it to whisper.” It’s already printed on forty billboards.
The freelance illustrator messages: “I’m in a different time zone, it’s night here, but I can finish for double the rate.” The illustration is needed by noon.
At the morning briefing the client says: “We want a viral video. Budget of one post. Deadline: yesterday.” The account manager is already nodding.
The retoucher brings in the juice packaging photo. The oranges look so perfect they seem plastic. Two hours until print.
left: Ask for a bit more realism
right: Ship it, the client will love it

text: The agency head gathers everyone at 9:00 and announces: “From today, no idea without a moodboard.” You’re running late for a client meeting.
right: Quietly slip off to the meeting

text: The plotter has chewed up the presentation print. It was the last sheet of large-format paper in the office. The showing is in forty minutes.
right: Show it on a laptop instead

text: The motion designer begs everyone not to touch his machine: “Nine-hour render, three left. Open a browser and it all crashes.” You urgently need a file from it.
left: Wait for the render to finish
right: Ask him to send the file now

text: The strategist sends 80 slides of research on “Who buys dumplings.” The key insight, on slide 79: “Hungry people.” The client presentation is at 11.
left: Cut it down to ten slides

text: At the review the client looks at the layout: “Good, but can it be more ‘wow’?” He can’t define “wow,” but he’ll know it when he sees it.
The brainstorm is in its second hour. There are 120 sticky notes on the board, 40 of them say “kittens.” The team lead suggests “no limits.” Lunch is getting cold.
An invitation to a tender arrives: big brand, creative task, one week. The work is unpaid, and one of twelve agencies will win.
left: Go for it with the whole team

text: The account manager asks you to “just sit in” on a client call “to make up the numbers.” It’s been 50 minutes, and nobody has asked you anything.
The client sends an edit: “Make the background white but not white. Like white, only warmer, and not beige.” The designer looks at you hopefully.
right: Call the client with a palette

text: The agency accountant reminds you that the client hasn’t paid for the last project in three months. Today they sent a new brief, “urgent, with love.”
left: Take it, but ask for prepayment

text: At a food shoot the photographer demands real hot soup, while the food stylist wants it cold “so it doesn’t sag.” There’s only one pot of soup.
The client on a call: “Can you remove the person from the photo? And the dog. And the house. Just leave the happiness.” It’s the campaign’s key visual.
The copywriter refuses to write about the “revolutionary” toothbrush: “It’s just a toothbrush. I won’t lie.” The client wants the word “revolution” three times.
The art director and the account manager are fighting in the meeting room: one calls the layout “art,” the other “something nobody will buy.” Both want you to settle it.
The media buyer says the banner with a cat got ten times more clicks than the one with the product. But the client sells building materials, not cats.
At a pet food shoot the dog actor refuses the food and eats the cameraman’s sandwich. Take 27, the set is rented until six.
left: Film the dog eating the sandwich

text: The client wants “all our advantages” on the packaging. There are 34. The packaging is a tea bag the size of a postage stamp.
The illustrator drew a mascot for a bank: a smiling hedgehog. The client likes it, but legal asks whether customers will feel “prickled by the loans.”
The mineral water brand’s post suddenly hit a million views because of a typo in “sparkling.” Commenters love it; the client is horrified.
left: Play along with a follow-up post

text: The agency CFO wants everyone to log timesheets in 15-minute blocks. You spend twenty minutes figuring out how to log “stared out the window looking for an idea.”
right: Log it honestly as window time

text: The intern accidentally sent the client a file named “layout_final_really_final_DO_NOT_SHOW.” The client replied: “This one is the best.”
right: Polish the draft into a final

text: 7:30 p.m. The creative director drops by: “Good idea, but let’s kill it and start over. I feel we can do better.” The presentation is tomorrow at ten.
9:15 p.m. The client writes: “I showed the layout to my wife, she doesn’t like the green.” It’s a hardware store chain, and green is their brand color.
right: Reply in the morning about the brand book

text: 2:47 a.m. The final video is exporting; the progress bar says “4 hours left,” though a minute ago it said “12 minutes.” Delivery is at 9:00.
It’s the evening of an advertising award ceremony. Your video is shortlisted, but the show is dragging on and you have a shoot at 8 a.m. Your category is last.
The freelance 3D artist has vanished with the files a day before delivery. Last message: “Gone inward, will be back.” His phone is off.
right: Ask the client for an extension

text: At home you tell the family about your day. They ask you to “draw something simple for auntie’s birthday.” You’ve been drawing all day.
At 8 p.m. the account manager calls: “The client wants to look at all options once more before bed. Can you put them in one PDF?” Six people have the options.
right: Offer to send it in the morning

text: After delivering the campaign the team suggests staying for board games at the office. You’ve slept five hours a night for three nights.
Late in the evening the client sends an 11-minute voice message. At the end: “So, all great, just change everything.”
In the evening, a page that mocks bad ads roasts your agency’s campaign. 2,000 comments, half of them about the font.
left: Reply with humor as the agency
right: Ignore it and wait it out

text: Late at night the designer sends the final with a note: “not sure about this.” It looks good, but there’s a stray layer in the corner called “test kitten.”
left: Delete the kitten and send it
right: Call the designer and praise him

text: Friday evening. The system wants your weekly timesheet. You only remember Monday, and that Tuesday had “something about juice.”
You stay late to hang work on the walls for tomorrow’s pitch guests. The cleaner politely mentions she’d like to go home too.
9:40 p.m. The courier with the printed packaging samples is stuck in traffic and asks you to meet him at a metro station across town.
right: Ask him to bring them in the morning

text: The creative director posts in the chat at 11 p.m.: “Guys, I’ve got it! Will tell you in the morning.” A minute later: “No, it was awful, forget it.”
left: Joke back and go to bed

text: Your desk neighbor, a motion designer, heads home and asks you to “just hit the button when the render hits 100.” It’s at 34%, and you were about to leave.
right: Leave a note and go home

text: Pitch day. In the client’s lobby you run into a rival agency carrying a huge mock-up in bubble wrap. Your whole pitch fits in a laptop.
Ten minutes before the pitch the slide clicker dies. The creative director says: “You’ll stand by the laptop and advance slides when I nod.”
right: Hunt for a battery in the client’s office

text: Morning pitch rehearsal. The creative director rewrites the opening line for the sixth time. Now it goes: “Imagine… no, don’t imagine.”
left: Suggest going back to version one

text: The client’s procurement team writes before office hours: “We like your estimate but need a 40% discount. Same scope.”
The intern turned up in a suit and tie because “it’s pitch day.” The rest of the team is in hoodies. The client makes formal suits.
left: Put the intern front and center
right: Ask him to lose the tie for vibe

text: In the metro you spot your own poster. Someone drew a mustache on the hero, and honestly, it’s an improvement. Snap a photo for the team?
left: Post it in the team chat
right: Report the vandalism to the client

text: The art director and copywriter, a creative duo, aren’t speaking and talk through you: “Tell him the headline is weak.” The pitch is in two days.
left: Make them sit down and talk

text: The client sends a photo of his office: “I want the ad to feel like this carpet.” The carpet is burgundy with swirly monograms.
right: Gently ask what he likes about it

text: First thing in the morning the agency lawyer says the “happy family” photo on the billboards was licensed for blog use only. The billboards are all over town.
right: Replace it with your own photo

text: The agency coffee machine is broken, and at 9:30 there’s a brainstorm for an energy bar brand. The team looks at you like a savior.
left: Run out for coffee for everyone

text: Turns out the font the whole campaign is built on is free for non-commercial use only. The license costs a month’s budget.
The account director invites you to a 7:30 breakfast with the client “for informal bonding.” You usually wake up at eight.
right: Suggest a call later in the day

text: Shoot day morning. The AD reports the prop truck went to the wrong location. Without it you have an empty kitchen and an actress.
right: Drive to fetch the props yourself

text: Halfway through the pitch the projector dies. The marketing director says: “Just tell us in words, it’s more fun anyway.”
left: Tell it like a bedtime story
right: Ask for five minutes to fix it

text: After the tender the client picks another agency. A month later you see their campaign: it’s your idea, in a different color.
right: Let it go and learn from it

text: The client asks why the media plan has so much late-night radio. The media buyer whispers that it’s cheaper at night and “someone’s always awake.”
The client says: “Do it like the competition, but so nobody can tell.” A printout of someone else’s ad lands on the table.
The client’s brand manager approves the layout. An hour later his boss cancels the approval. An hour after that, the boss’s boss brings back the first version.
The team invites you to lunch, but you have edits due at three. The café next door has a soup of the day “in honor of your ad.”
The sound engineer wants another voice-over take: “The word ‘delicious’ sounded sad.” It’s take 41, and the voice actor is on his third tea.
At the review the client asks: “Can the video be shorter but keep everything?” It runs 30 seconds; they need 6.
The production company’s estimate includes a line called “unforeseen inspiration” — 15% of the budget. Everything else looks fine.
left: Ask them to explain that line

text: The blogger you hired filmed an integration where she mixes up the brand name. It’s funny, and the video is already gaining views.
The office manager asks the creatives to name the new meeting room. The team’s suggestions: “The Bunker,” “Client Tears” and “One More Edit.”
During an online client review you share the wrong window. On screen: the team chat discussing his tie.
The agency head wants to enter your campaign for an award, which needs a case video with “results.” There are none yet — it launched yesterday.
right: Make a video about the “bold vision”

text: The client’s lawyer wants an 18-second disclaimer on a kids’ juice ad. The ad is 15 seconds long.
left: Speed the text up to a squeak

text: The printer calls: the furniture catalog spread shows a cat instead of the sofa it was sleeping on during the shoot. Print run: 20,000.
At the brainstorm a quiet layout artist mumbles an idea better than anything so far. The creative director didn’t hear and repeats it louder as his own.
left: Say out loud whose idea it was

text: The client wants his son in the ad: “He’s very artistic.” The son is a serious teenager who clearly doesn’t want to be filmed.
right: Persuade the client to cast an actor

text: The client is rebranding from “Window World” to “Window World.” The difference: the letter O is now rounder. They want a presentation about “the revolution.”
left: Find meaning in the rounder O

text: 11:40 p.m. Someone spots a wrong digit in the client’s phone number on the final banner. The banners go to print at 8 a.m.
left: Fix it and wake the printers
right: Fix it and wait for morning

text: In the evening the creative director asks you to “just sketch a couple of ideas by morning, nothing serious.” Tomorrow he’ll show them to the client as finished work.
The agency is celebrating a tender win. The DJ is the accountant, and the music is the agency anthem in five arrangements. You’ve been dreaming of silence.
8:30 p.m. The client sends a new 140-page brand book: “Take it into account for tomorrow’s review.” The review is at 10 a.m.
A freelance copywriter asks to be paid “now, while my soul’s register is still open.” The copy isn’t in yet, but it’s promised by morning.
At night the render farm reports an error at 99%. The log says: “not enough memory.” The motion designer is asleep with his phone on silent.
right: Go to bed and wait till morning

text: In the evening the family is watching TV, and your ad comes on. Everyone turns: “You made this? Why is the dog sad?”
In the evening the account manager writes: “The client is on vacation but wants everything emailed so he can review by the pool.” 48 options, 200 MB each.
At the award ceremony the host reads out the winner in your category — your agency. The creative director is stuck in traffic. You have to go on stage.
left: Go up and thank the team
right: Ask them to present it later

text: In the evening the designer says he’s “burned out and can’t look at blue anymore.” The whole bank campaign is blue, and the final edits are tomorrow.
left: Take on the blue edits yourself
right: Give him a day off and push the deadline

text: 1 a.m. Just you and an intern left, finishing a storyboard. He says he’s afraid to go home: “What if the client changes his mind by morning.”
The night before the tender deadline a partner suggests “slightly embellishing” the past client list. The café on the corner was your client once.
Overnight the brand account you run gets a comment: “Your banner is so scary I’m no longer afraid of the dark.” Thousands of likes.
You finally made it to the gym, but your own ad is playing on the treadmill screen, and your phone buzzes: it’s the client.
right: Finish the workout and call back

text: Cycling to work, you come up with the best slogan of the year. The only way to write it down is to stop in the middle of traffic.
left: Pull over and write it down
right: Memorize it by chanting out loud

text: Morning: 300 unread messages in the agency chat. 280 are birthday stickers, 20 are urgent edits buried somewhere in between.
left: Scroll through all of it carefully

text: The client drops by unannounced at 9:05: “Was in the area, thought I’d watch the creative being born.” Nothing’s born yet; everyone is drinking coffee.
right: Park him in a meeting room with cookies

text: In the morning the creative director requests a moodboard about “the feeling of Monday, but positive.” You look out at the rain and search for positivity.
left: Build a moodboard out of rain
right: Ask him to clarify the mood

text: Friday evening. The agency head announces a “creative Saturday”: repainting the office walls in “the color of ideas.” The color hasn’t been chosen yet.
5:30 a.m. on a set in a field. The generator won’t start, and the sunrise everyone came for is in twenty minutes.
left: Shoot the dawn with natural light
right: Fix the generator as a crew

text: The casting director brought three actors for the role of “typical dad.” All three are the same man in different wigs. “It’s cheaper,” she says.
At the porridge ad shoot the child actor declares he hates porridge and demands pancakes. His mom says he’s “in character.”
The makeup artist is sick and can’t come. The actor is supposed to look “perfectly rested.” He looks like he just got off a red-eye.
right: Rewrite the scene as “morning after a flight”

text: The commercial director shows up with a new idea: “Let’s shoot everything backwards, end to start.” The script is client-approved.
The owner of the apartment where you’re shooting a “cozy home” ad asks you not to move furniture, not to turn on lights and “not to breathe on the ficus.”
The catering is two hours late. A crew of forty is hungry and eyeing the prop croissants.
right: Order pizza on your own dime

text: The freelance editor sends his cut at 7 a.m. with a note: “I reinterpreted the piece.” It’s now black and white and about loneliness. It’s a dumpling ad.
left: Ask for the original cut back
right: Show the client the bold version

text: You’re on a commuter train to an out-of-town shoot. A vendor in the carriage pitches flashlights better than you’ve ever pitched anything. Take notes?
The client decided to come to the shoot personally. At 8 a.m. he’s already on set giving the cameraman orders. The cameraman gives you a “save me” look.
right: Let him direct, it’s his money

text: The forecast promised sunshine, but it’s snowing. The May picnic commercial is shooting today, and the park rental is only paid for today.
The crew bus driver is lost. The GPS is routing everyone through a river ford. The driver says: “I’ll risk it if you say so.”
right: Call taxis for the whole crew

text: The cameraman arrives with a brand-new camera he hasn’t tried: “We’ll figure out how it works today.” There’s one shoot and no reshoots.
The stylist brought clothes for the lead. Everything is three sizes too small. Stores open at ten; the shoot starts at nine.
right: Shoot in the actress’s own clothes

text: For the “busy street” scene, four extras out of thirty showed up. The director asks the whole crew to “walk back and forth.”
The dog actor’s trainer warns that he only performs to a certain song. Only her husband knows it, and he’s at work.
Noon on set. The neighbor’s rooster keeps wandering into frame and crowing at the end of every take. The rooster’s owner wants a fee.
left: Pay up and feature the rooster
right: Move the camera to another corner

text: The producer says you’re going into overtime. Every extra hour costs an intern’s weekly salary. Two key shots are left.
right: Shoot one, do the other in graphics

text: The lead actress in the yogurt commercial confesses she’s lactose intolerant. The scene has her eating a spoonful with a blissful smile.
left: Swap the yogurt for fruit purée

text: After take twenty the client on set says: “Let’s go back to the first take, it felt more alive.” The first take was shot without sound.
The drone operator wants an aerial shot over the client’s office. Turns out flying there isn’t allowed, and without the aerial the ending falls apart.
The screenwriter suggests a twist: “And at the end, it turns out it was all the vacuum cleaner’s dream.” The client sells vacuum cleaners.
left: Pitch the twist to the client

text: Construction starts next to the set. The jackhammer fires up exactly between your takes, as if it had its own director.
The props master bought plastic food for the “family dinner” scene. On camera it gleams like Christmas ornaments. The nearest store is 20 minutes away.
An assistant on set mixed up the clapperboard, so every take is labeled “scene 1.” The editor will later face 64 “scene ones.”
left: Rewrite the shot log by hand
right: Leave it as a quest for the editor

text: A guest blogger on set is filming behind-the-scenes for her followers. The client’s unreleased product is visible in the background.
left: Ask her to delete the video
right: Turn it into an official teaser

text: While you were on the shoot, the agency held another client meeting without you. The minutes say: “Agreed you’ll do everything by Thursday.”
right: Reply that timelines are up for discussion

text: The client watches the take on the monitor and wants “a bit more emotion.” The actor is already crying, laughing and shouting in one shot.
right: Show the client all takes in a row

text: The cameraman discovers all the morning footage has a smudge on the lens. It’s heart-shaped — someone touched the glass.
The studio calls: their next booking is at 4 p.m.; yours ends at 3. It’s 2:20, and you’ve shot half.
right: Ask the studio to bump the others

text: The stand-in who was supposed to “run across wet asphalt” backs out at the last minute. That leaves the actor, the director and you, in sneakers.
The sun is down, but the client wants “one more take at sunset.” There’s no sunset left; it’s a chilly autumn evening, and the crew is freezing.
right: Wrap and send the crew home

text: 10 p.m. The editor wants you to see the first cut. It’s set to music the client flatly banned. It sounds perfect.
right: Send it to the client and risk it

text: After the shoot the producer wants an expense report with receipts. Your pocket holds one gum receipt and a note: “taxi, about 1200.”
right: Hand it in as is with a note

text: You’re heading home after a 14-hour shoot. The director offers you a lift, but wants to “debrief while it’s fresh” on the way.
right: Take a cab and enjoy silence

text: 9:30 p.m. The client sends a photo he took on set with his phone and asks for “this shot for the ending.” It’s the back of the cameraman’s head.
left: Find a similar shot in the footage

text: The freelance colorist writes in the evening: “I graded it to a Northern European mood.” The summer lemonade ad is now grey-blue.
left: Ask him to bring back summer

text: After the shoot you’re left with 200 bottles of prop kvass that can’t be returned. The producer suggests giving them to everyone “as a souvenir.”
right: Donate them to a shelter nearby

text: Midnight. The client wants to see a “rough cut” in the morning. The footage is still copying from memory cards, which will take three hours.
In the evening, forty people in the crew chat argue about who left a tripod on set. It’s rented, and everyone is looking for it except whoever left it.
You get home at 11 p.m. after the shoot to find the dishwasher broken. The sink is piled high, and tomorrow is another early start.
The director calls at midnight: “Can’t sleep. I think we shot a masterpiece. Or a disaster. Tell me it’s a masterpiece.”
In the evening accounts say they can’t pay the rooster from the shoot: “There’s no budget line for ‘rooster services.’”
Right before bed you remember you never checked whether the car-priced lens was returned to the rental house. The assistant isn’t answering.
After the shoot the actress writes that she was filmed from “the wrong side of her face.” She wants a reshoot or she’ll block the ad.
In the edit suite you discover the ad runs 34 seconds. Airtime is 30. Every second is somebody’s favorite.
At home your own dog turns away in offense: you smell of the dog actor from set. She won’t even take a treat.
left: Make up with a long walk

text: The creative director writes after the shoot: “Great day! Reshoot of the ending at seven tomorrow, I dreamed a better version.”
right: Ask him to sketch the dream first

text: You’re editing at home late at night with headphones on, but the neighbors bang on the wall: apparently you’ve been singing along to the jingle. Loudly.
right: Gift them a copy of the ad

text: The client’s press office wants every character in the ad to wear a company badge. The scene is a family dinner at home.
left: Stick the badges on the fridge
right: Talk them out of the badges

text: You wake up to find the plumbing ad you made “just to tick a box” has five million views. Your phone is exploding.
The creative director arrives in a T-shirt that says “No Ideas.” He calls it a performance to motivate the team. The team looks tense.
The awards shortlist comes out. Your work isn’t on it, but the agency next door is — with an idea you once tossed them over lunch.
You launched a hashtag challenge for a vacuum brand. Overnight it got two videos: one from the intern’s mom and one from the intern.
The top comment under the client’s ad post: “Whoever came up with this, give them an award.” Right below: “Or fire them.” The client asks which is right.
The intern proposed running the dairy brand’s account in the voice of a cow. In a week it has more followers than the dairy itself.
The client writes: “Our ad became a meme. But people are laughing at our CEO in the shot, not at the joke.” The CEO doesn’t know yet.
The awards organizers remind you today is the last day for entries. Each category costs as much as a new laptop. You have five pieces.
You’ve been invited on a morning TV show to talk about your viral campaign. Airtime 7:15, and you are not a morning person.
The freelancer who animated the viral clip writes: “Saw it went big. Can I be credited? And get a bonus?”
Your creative duo both want to be named in “Best Copywriting.” The rules allow only one author.
The agency analyst shows a chart: the campaign went massively viral, but the client’s sales didn’t budge. The client hasn’t seen it yet.
right: Wait a week, maybe sales will move

text: Your meme banner for a bakery chain went viral, but people are remixing it with competing bakeries. The client’s lawyers are nervous.
The agency head calls a morning meeting: “We need a viral hit by the end of the month. Any. Who’s in?” Silence in the room.
The brand wants a live unboxing of their new frying pan. The host: the brand’s own director. He’s never been on camera.
On your morning run you see people in the park doing the dance from your ad. Someone is doing it wrong.
left: Go show them the right moves

text: The award jury invites you to present your work. You get five minutes; the deck runs twenty. You need to cut it now, in the taxi.
The video that ate the whole budget got 312 views in a week. 200 of them were the agency and client teams.
left: Admit it flopped at the meeting

text: A blogger with a million followers offers a free integration if the brand names the product after him. The product is a drain cleaner.
left: Pass the offer to the client

text: The client wants a viral video “but nothing silly, no jokes, no animals and no people.” That leaves the product on a white background.
right: Ask to bring back one of the “no’s”

text: The community manager is frazzled: an argument broke out under the brand’s post about what color the dress in the photo is. The brand sells shoes.
right: Pin a post about the shoes

text: A rival agency publishes a case study naming your viral video as their “inspiration.” Their case got more likes than your video.
The report shows the ad gets its best reach at 3:40 a.m. The client wants to know who’s watching and asks for an audience profile.
The creatives want to make an “anti-ad” — a video about why nobody should buy the client’s product. They swear it’s a guaranteed hit.
left: Pitch the bravery to the client

text: The agency decided to start a video blog. Episode one: “A Day in the Life” of you. Your day is spreadsheets and edits.
left: Play a jazzier version of yourself

text: The client forwards someone else’s viral video: “I want one like this.” It was filmed by accident and shows a raccoon stealing cookies.
A flash mob for a sneaker brand is planned in the square. Twelve dancers showed up — and eleven security guards asking for permits.
right: Move it to the office courtyard

text: Your slogan was translated for the international campaign. In one language it reads as “Buy a little sadness.”
The media agency reports the campaign reach is “within normal range.” Your creative director demands the word “breakthrough” in the press release.
The client asks whether the whole campaign could be generated by AI “for half the price.” Your designers are sitting right there, hearing it.
Your billboard joking about traffic jams went up right above the city’s worst traffic jam. Drivers photograph it and post angry rants at you.
right: Apologize on behalf of the brand

text: A trade journalist wants an interview about “the secret of virality.” The honest answer is “luck,” but you can’t write an article about that.
Awards night. You won bronze, but on stage the mic goes to the agency head, who hadn’t even seen the work before submission.
right: Say a few words about the team

text: 10 p.m. The video suddenly blew up, and the client wants “a sequel overnight while it’s hot.” The team has gone home.
right: Make a quick reaction post yourself

text: After the awards there’s an after-party with every creative director in town. You could network — or go home and sleep.
You’re carrying the award trophy home on the metro. It’s heavy and pointy, and people stare. One passenger asks if it’s stolen.
In the evening social media calls your campaign “the worst ad of the year.” Your personal account is tagged in twenty posts.
left: Lock your account for the night
right: Read it all and sort the criticism

text: The agency head sends a voice message: “We urgently need an awards case video. Deadline 9 a.m. tomorrow. You edit cases better than anyone.”
At dinner your friends discuss “that dumb ad with the talking toaster.” It’s yours. Tell them?
After the campaign flops the client writes: “We’re disappointed. But let’s try again — you have a week and half the money.”
right: Ask for an honest debrief first

text: After the campaign flops the team sits in silence. Someone suggests a “wake for the idea” with a cake shaped like the client’s logo.
At 1:30 a.m. the intern posts fifty ideas “for the next viral campaign” in the group chat. All of them involve dancing penguins.
right: Reply now and send him to bed

text: Your project won a grand prix — in the category “Most Absurd Ad of the Year.” The client doesn’t know whether to celebrate or be offended.
You’re invited on an evening ad podcast. The host wants “spicy client stories.” You have plenty, but clients might listen.
Your mom calls in the evening: “Saw your ad! Why is the font so small? Make it bigger, people can’t see it.”
Dozens of brands copied your video. In the evening the client asks: “Why is everyone doing what we did, but people buy from them?”
The agency decides to hang your award certificate in the restroom, “so everyone sees it.” You’re not sure it’s a compliment.
left: Ask for a spot in the lobby

text: Friday evening. No client has written for two hours. Suspicious. Check email again or switch off the phone?
In the morning the agency assistant reports your viral campaign has “leaked” into someone else’s deck: a nearby agency is showing it to clients as their own.
In the evening the awards email you: your entry is disqualified because it aired a day after the cutoff. The team is still celebrating the shortlist.
Morning notification: the client paid the invoice. Half of it, with a note: “The rest once we feel the effect of the logo.”
The account manager wants the estimate redone: “The client likes lots of lines with small amounts.” The total must stay the same.
The freelance illustrator sends a contract where clause 14 reads: “The client may not call my work ‘cute.’”
The client ordered one banner. Over two weeks he “just added” a website, three videos and next year’s calendar. Same budget.
left: Do it all for the relationship

text: The agency CFO announces savings: the stock photo subscription is cancelled. Today’s campaign is built entirely from stock photos.
A freelance animator asks to be paid in crypto “because banks make me sad.” Accounts can’t do that.
right: Say no and look for someone else

text: The account director says the client will raise the budget if the agency comes up with a name for his country house “as a bonus.”
You realize you’ve been paying for the agency’s cloud storage out of pocket for three months. The total is not small.
right: Move projects to the office server

text: A tender platform manager writes: to bid on the logo contest you need 47 documents, including proof that your interns have no debts.
The bank blocked a payment to a freelancer because the reference said “for a funny head for the chicken.” It was a character for an ad.
The client offers “equity in the startup” instead of payment. The startup is an app that counts your cat’s steps. Two users so far.
The CFO points out that 400 hours were logged on the bakery client but only 80 were billed. He asks where the hours went.
A talented freelancer asks you to recommend him to another agency. If he goes, you’ll miss him.
The production company wants 100% upfront. The client pays the agency only after airing. The agency would have to front its own money.
The courier service billed you for delivering a mock-up to the client’s office next door. Turns out the courier took it across town and back.
The agency is giving clients branded candles “Scented Like a Deadline” for the holidays. You’re asked to define what a deadline smells like.
The client at a meeting: “Why does the logo cost so much? It’s just a letter in a circle.” You spent three weeks on that letter.
right: Joke about the price of circles

text: The freelance photographer billed you for “emotional damages from photographing aspic.” Small amount, but the wording will baffle accounts.
right: Ask him to reissue the invoice

text: The client’s procurement team wants every line of the video budget explained. They’re especially curious about the “fog” line — why fog costs so much.
Accounts rejected your report: the props receipt says “one inflatable flamingo, qty 3.” They need a proper invoice.
left: Go back to the store for paperwork
right: Log the flamingos as a gift

text: A major client is ready to sign a yearly contract, but wants you personally to answer his calls at any hour.
An outdoor ad contractor offers you a kickback for choosing his billboards. His billboards are actually good, and you’d have picked them anyway.
You find your idea in a freelancer’s portfolio, credited to him. He only did the final illustration for it.
left: Ask him to fix the credit

text: The client wants a video estimate “in three versions: expensive, normal and like last time.” Last time was free, at a pitch.
The agency head asks why you passed on a near-free project from a “promising client.” The client offers “exposure instead of money.”
The client announced a tender, but the winner is obvious: his son-in-law’s agency. You’ve been invited anyway, “for competition.”
right: Submit strong work out of spite

text: A freelancer you still owe money from the last project offers his services again. Accounts is holding up the payment for reasons of its own.
The client wants a discount because “the logo came out small.” According to the brand book, it’s supposed to be small.
right: Show the brand book and refuse

text: Mid-project the client halves the budget but asks to “keep the same level.” The creative team already bought props.
left: Rebuild the project at half scale

text: An acquaintance offers you a side gig: a logo for his coffee shop, evenings, cash. Your agency normally charges big money for that.
right: Refer the coffee shop to the agency

text: An agent offers a “top illustrator” at the price of three regular ones. The portfolio has a single piece: a self-portrait with a cat.
left: Test him on a small task

text: The client asks for all source files “just in case.” Per the contract, source files cost extra, and he knows that.
Friday evening email: the client refuses to pay because “the ad is good but overall unsuccessful.” It’s already on air.
left: Draft a claim over the weekend

text: At 10 p.m. a freelancer sends the work and asks to be paid “right now or I won’t sleep.” It’s good, with two small mistakes.
In the evening you book your vacation. That same minute an email arrives: the client scheduled the campaign launch for the middle of your trip.
right: Keep it and hand over tasks

text: The agency head writes in the evening: “Salaries delayed a week, clients aren’t paying. We stick together!” The team chat is anxious.
right: Ask the head for an explanation

text: At home you add up expenses and realize the coffee near the agency cost more this month than your utilities.
Late in the evening the client offers “barter”: spa passes instead of part of the payment. The team hasn’t rested in ages.
left: Take passes for the whole team

text: A freelancer vanished after the advance. In the evening you find him online posting beach photos captioned “finally, no deadlines.”
right: Tell him what you really think

text: In the evening you remember the tax return for last year’s side gig is due tomorrow. The documents are somewhere in your inbox among the edits.
right: Ask a friend who’s an accountant

text: Your evening coffee-shop client asks you to “also do the menu.” It’s the third free extra. You’re tired.
right: Quote a price for the menu

text: At 9 p.m. the account manager asks to redo the estimate because the client “doesn’t like the number at the end.” That number is the total.
The agency head announces in the evening: the quarterly bonus will be paid in “experience and gratitude.” The team exchanges looks.
left: Joke that you can’t eat experience
right: Stay quiet and wait it out

text: Late at night you read the new client contract. Clause 38: “The agency agrees to unlimited revisions.” Signing is tomorrow morning.
left: Strike the clause and risk it

text: The client sent the agency a thank-you fruit basket. The note inside: “Tomorrow we’ll discuss why everything needs redoing.”
You paid for the crew’s taxis on your own card all shoot week. No reimbursement yet, but the cashback covers exactly one kebab.
An agency partner offers you equity — on condition that you “work even more.” You already work until midnight.
Morning news: the client paid not you but an agency with a similar name across the street. They haven’t said a word.
A freelance type designer offers to create a custom font for the client. It’ll take a month and bump the budget, but it’ll be gorgeous.
An evening statement shows the agency card paid for a horoscope service for cats. Suspicion falls on you — you had the card at the shoot.
right: Pay it yourself and forget it

text: The designer insists the logo is perfect turquoise on his monitor. On yours it’s green; on the client’s, light blue. It prints today.
left: Go to the printer for a proof

text: First thing in the morning the agency cloud warns: “Storage full.” The last upload is a video as big as an entire film library.
You’re looking for the final layout and find: “final,” “final2,” “final_for_real,” “final_fixed_client,” “NOT THIS ONE.” Which to send?
The printer calls at 8:15: “Your file’s in the wrong color mode for print. The colors will shift.” It’s a campaign for a bright toy chain.
The designer refuses to work on the new computer: “The old one knew my habits.” The old one went to accounts.
right: Help set up the new one

text: Overnight the layout software updated itself and now won’t open yesterday’s files. The brochure is due at 11.
The account manager asks the designer to fix a font in a deck “for a minute.” The designer says it’s the twentieth “minute” this morning.
right: Ask the designer to help anyway

text: Nobody at the agency remembers the client’s brand account password. A post is due at 10:00. The last person who knew it quit in spring.
The art director bought a new font and wants it in every project. Even in the client’s accounting report.
Your laptop won’t turn on the morning of the presentation. It holds the deck you, naturally, never backed up.
left: Rush it to a repair shop

text: Morning call with the client: your audio drops, and you watch him gesture through something important for half an hour.
right: Nod along and wait for the minutes

text: The office printer prints everything pink. The sysadmin says: “It’s not a bug, it’s a mood.” You have a meeting with a serious bank today.
The intern found a way to make file export three times faster. Except now every file is named after him.
right: Ask him to refine it first

text: The sysadmin reports backups haven’t run in six months. Nothing was lost, but if anything had been, everything would have been.
right: Laugh it off and move on

text: The designer sent a layout signed “This is a masterpiece, no edits accepted.” The brand name has a typo.
The client sent his morning edits… as a phone photo of his monitor, with circles drawn on it by finger.
The account manager and designer argue over who’s to blame for the billboard typo. One sent the text, the other typed it. The billboards are up.
left: Take the blame for the department

text: The designer wants a new tablet at the price of two old ones: “The old one has no inspiration in it.” The CFO wants your opinion.
The client is breaking his own brand book: he wants the logo on purple, which page 12 forbids in all caps.
The account manager promised the client the designer would “draw a mascot in an hour.” The designer is hearing it from you.
At the all-hands, account managers complain creatives don’t answer the chat. Creatives complain account managers post every three minutes.
The designer plays music for inspiration. Next door, the account managers are negotiating with a client to his soundtrack.
left: Ask him to turn it down

text: The account manager forwarded the client’s email to the designer verbatim, including “your designer clearly didn’t try.” The designer is in tears.
The client asks the designer directly, bypassing the account manager: “Can I get your number to speed things up?” The account manager doesn’t know.
right: Route it all back through accounts

text: The art director holds a “post-mortem” on every layout: forty minutes per banner. Eighteen banners are queued today.
The layout artist says the text overruns by 40 characters. The copywriter won’t cut a letter: “Every word was suffered for.”
The agency’s sales team promised a client an “animated logo with a voice.” The creatives are hearing for the first time that logos talk.
The creatives ask to ban account managers from brainstorms: “They immediately ask how much it costs.” The account managers are offended.
The designer made fifteen versions when three were requested. The client has been unable to choose for a week.
right: Give the client time to decide

text: The account manager asks creatives to call “edits” “wishes” in all correspondence. It’s his new methodology.
right: Joke about it at the all-hands

text: The designer grabbed an image from the internet “temporarily, for the mock-up.” The client approved it and is sending it to print with that photo.
right: Swap the photo and come clean

text: The campaign master file is so heavy it takes half an hour to open. Everyone sighs when opening it. Nobody dares change anything.
The client is puzzled: “Why do you need a designer if my nephew draws on a tablet?” The nephew sends a logo drawn as a dragon.
right: Use the dragon as a starting point

text: 11 p.m. The computer says: “Not enough disk space.” To continue the render you’ll have to delete something. Like five years of your personal photos.
In the evening you accidentally reply to the client in the chat where you were discussing him: “Here he goes with his purple again.” Delivered.
right: Pretend it was about someone else

text: The designer messages in the evening: “I’m going freelance. Tomorrow is my last day.” He ran three key projects.
right: Wish him well and take over

text: At 10:30 p.m. the account manager asks for a “tiny edit”: change one color in the deck. It’s used on 140 slides.
In the evening you migrate to a new computer and forget the fonts. In the morning every layout will look like a school newspaper.
At 11 p.m. the creative director deletes “everything unnecessary” from the shared folder. In the morning it’ll turn out that included the final files.
right: Check the trash in the morning

text: You stay overnight to finish a deck. The office coffee machine is broken again, and the nearest 24-hour shop is closed for repairs.
right: Go home and get up at five

text: The sysadmin announces there’ll be no internet tomorrow 9 to 12: “Scheduled maintenance.” You have an online pitch at 10.
The final client report is ready. You hit “send” and realize you attached your weekend grocery list instead.
At home your kid is coloring in the printout of a layout you brought home “to see with fresh eyes.” It came out brighter than the designer’s.
left: Snap a photo for the team

text: 1 a.m. Just you and the designer left. He offers to “quickly” redo the logo the client already approved: “I see how to make it better.”
In the evening the client created a group chat with the agency and invited his mom “so she can keep an eye on the creative.” She’s already sending edits.
Your phone offers to update overnight. Last time it wiped all your idea notes.
In the evening the client writes: “Send me the source file, I want to move things around a bit myself.” You picture what his “moving around” will do.
right: Offer a call to make edits together

text: Your noise-cancelling headphones broke. Without them, thinking in the open-plan agency is impossible. New ones cost a week of lunch money.
right: Make do and work from home

text: The client brings materials on a flash drive he got at a trade fair in 2009. None of the agency’s computers can read it.
left: Dig out an old laptop from storage
right: Ask him to email the files

text: An evening email: “Your password for all work services has expired.” The new one needs 14 characters, a special symbol and can’t repeat the last 30.
Brainstorm at 9:00. The creative director declares: “There are no bad ideas.” Ten minutes later the accountant, popping in for tea, suggests an ad shaped like a crossword.
The client’s brief is a single line: “Make it good.” He suggests asking clarifying questions “after he sees something.”
The client wants “eco-friendly” on packaging made of three kinds of plastic. The agency lawyer is silent; the client is in a hurry.
Your morning starts with a genius idea in the shower. While drying off, it slipped away. All that’s left is the word “penguin.”
left: Sit down and try to recall it
right: Let it go and have breakfast

text: The intern has been silent at three brainstorms in a row. Afterwards he leaves you a note with five great ideas.
right: Present them in his name yourself

text: At 8:30 the creative director sends a voice note: “An idea is death. We need an anti-idea.” Brainstorm at 9:00, topic: a new chip flavor.
The agency introduced morning meditation for creativity. Twenty minutes of silence while forty unanswered emails run around your head.
You walk to the office “for inspiration.” No inspiration, but you’re 15 minutes late to your own brainstorm.
left: Call and tell them to start

text: The creatives hung a sign: “Do not enter: idea being born.” Account managers are waiting outside with a client question.
right: Keep the door shut an hour

text: The client wants a customer contest for the best slogan. The prize: a year’s supply of the product. The product is salt.
The client suggests “helping” his café reviews a little: writing twenty glowing ones as “guests.” He says everyone does it.
right: Propose a real promo for guests

text: The office has a new “idea wall.” Overnight someone replaced every sticky note with drawings of ducks. Honestly, the ducks are funny.
left: Make ducks the theme of the week

text: The agency brought in a psychologist to help the team with burnout. The first session is at 9 a.m. on a major delivery day.
The client wants copy saying his juicer “will save your marriage.” His own legal team asks for proof.
Morning office yoga. The instructor asks you to “release all thoughts.” Your thoughts are about a logo that needs to be bigger.
Monday morning. In your inbox, an email from the client sent Sunday at 11:58 p.m.: “All great!” Nothing else.
At the brainstorm everyone pitches the same idea in different words. The creative director says: “Great, we have seven ideas!”
The client wants a candy ad where kids “persuade” parents to buy it. The creative team is split down the middle.
At the brainstorm the intern pitches an idea you recognize: an ad that won an award five years ago. He’s sure he came up with it.
right: Say nothing and skip the idea

text: The bank client wants the fine print removed from the ad: “It ruins the picture.” Without it, the ad is misleading.
The creative director asks everyone to whisper ideas at the brainstorm, “so as not to scare them off.” The client is watching on video and can’t hear a thing.
You find an ad online strikingly similar to the one your team delivers the day after tomorrow. The team swears they never saw it.
At lunch you go for a walk without your phone — first time in a month. You come back to 89 messages and “Where are you?”
right: Say you were walking and breathe

text: The copywriter brings a slogan you love. Later it turns out to be a line from a popular song.
right: Look into rights for the line

text: The client wants “bold provocation” in the ad, but “nobody can be offended.” He suggests starting with kittens.
Your creative team proposes an ad entirely in sign language, with subtitles. Bold and inclusive — but the client loves loud jingles.
The strategist claims the key insight for milk ads is “people miss their childhood.” The account manager thinks the insight is “milk is white.”
Your head is boiling. A colleague suggests fifteen minutes of table tennis. The client expects an answer in an hour.
The art director brings a moodboard for kids’ porridge ads. It’s all black-and-white photos of abandoned factories. “It’s about morning energy,” he explains.
left: Ask him to explain the link

text: The client proudly announces he wrote the slogan himself: “Our bread is bread.” He wants it on everything.
A rival agency invites you to a joint brainstorm “to share experience.” Suspiciously, it’s a week before a tender you’re both in.
The creatives have sat in silence staring at walls for half an hour. The agency head walks in and asks if anyone is working.
Two creatives argue over who came up with the idea first: “I said ‘cat,’ he said ‘in a hat.’” The idea is a cat in a hat.
A vitamin maker wants copy saying the product “cures fatigue.” It’s advertising, not medicine, and you can’t claim that.
1 a.m., and you can’t sleep: a toothpaste jingle is looping in your head. It’s horribly catchy and possibly genius.
The evening before your vacation the client sends a new brief: “We trust only you.” It’s due in a week — mid-vacation.
The creative director calls a brainstorm for 7 p.m., “because the brain is freer in the evening.” Half the team has kids in daycare until seven.
You decided not to answer after eight. At 8:05 the phone rings: “Client (don’t answer after 8).”
right: Let it ring and call back tomorrow

text: In the evening the creative director confides he’s exhausted and not sure he still loves advertising. He asks you not to tell anyone.
You signed up for an evening pottery class to unwind. The teacher asks you to sculpt “what worries you.” You sculpt a logo.
right: Make a vase and switch off

text: Friday, 9 p.m. You catch yourself reading the same brief sentence for the fifth time without understanding a word.
In the evening you watch a documentary about legendary ad people and feel you’ve achieved nothing. Tomorrow: six banners for a tire shop.
right: Look back at your old work

text: At home during a movie’s ad break, you instinctively start reviewing every commercial out loud. Your family asks you to stop.
In the evening a travel client asks you to “slightly embellish” a hotel in the ad — add a sea that isn’t there.
left: Refuse to paint in a sea

text: You dream that the client asks for a bigger logo, and you keep enlarging it until it blots out the sun. Alarm in an hour.
left: Get up early and take a walk

text: A neighbor finds out you work in advertising and asks for help with a lost cat poster. Judging by the photo, the cat left out of boredom.
In the evening someone in the team chat asks: “Does anyone remember why we’re doing this?” The message gets fifteen likes.
Walking home, you see passers-by smiling at your ad at a bus stop. You want to ask them what made them laugh.
Lately all your ideas look like your old ones. Tonight you could visit a museum or redo the deck one more time.
Before bed you write tomorrow’s to-do list. It runs two pages, and item one is “don’t forget to rest.”
A property developer wants the housing ad to show a park, a school and a waterfront. So far the site is a pit and one sad excavator.
The car dealership owner wants to star in the ad himself, driving into a sunset. He got his license a month ago.
left: Shoot it in a parked car

text: The restaurant chef won’t let a food stylist touch his dishes: “My food needs no makeup.” On camera it looks like a cafeteria photo.
right: Win the chef over to a stylist

text: A gym chain wants an ad that makes people “want to get up at 6 a.m.” You barely made it up at eight.
left: Make it honest about the struggle

text: A pet store ordered an ad where a parrot says the slogan. The parrot knows one word, and it’s the name of a competing pet store.
A serious bank wants a “youthful” ad. The marketing director asks for “words teenagers use.” His son made him the list in 2015.
left: Check the words with real teens

text: The owner of a family bakery brings a photo of her grandmother, the founder, and wants her as the face of the brand. Grandma hates being photographed.
A dental chain wants an ad “without fear.” Somehow every idea you have includes the sound of a drill, and the team winces.
right: Play the drill sound for laughs

text: A furniture factory wants its sofa advertised “like a luxury brand.” The sofa squeaks. You can hear it in every test shot.
right: Tell the client about the squeak

text: On a holiday morning the flower shop owner wants an urgent ad “for today.” She has flowers for three bouquets left.
left: Talk her out of the ad

text: An online sock store wants an ad that “really touches people.” Budget: one social media post.
right: Offer a series paid in installments

text: A patisserie wants their cake advertised “like celebrity wedding cakes.” It costs less than lunch at the café next door.
A language school wants a slogan in a foreign language. Their teacher found three mistakes in your version. He’s right about two.
right: Fix two and explain the third

text: The car wash owner wants the ad to “sparkle.” Literally — he asks for a banner with glitter. The printer doesn’t do that.
A private kindergarten requests an ad and sends kids’ drawings “for inspiration.” One drawing is your logo — only better.
right: Draw your own based on it

text: A vet clinic wants an ad where a cat says “Thank you, doctor.” Judging by his glare, the cat actor is not grateful.
A new client admits at the first meeting he “has never done advertising and is scared.” He’s almost in tears over the estimate.
A café chain wants all menu items renamed “creatively” for the campaign. Waiters can’t pronounce “Mousse of Dawn Mist.”
right: Keep them and add pronunciation tips

text: The soda client suddenly wants a “heartfelt” ad about grannies. The whole campaign so far has been extreme sports and skateboarders.
right: Talk him out of the pivot

text: A tour operator wants an ad for trips “for people who are tired.” You look at your team and realize it’s the perfect focus group.
The jeweler wants the ring in the ad to look “the size of a planet.” The photographer says macro photography isn’t magic.
right: Show the ring at real size

text: A taxi company wants an ad for “the fastest taxi.” Your driver for the shoot was two hours late.
left: Make a joke of the delay

text: A tire maker wants an ad that makes tires “emotional.” In the meeting everyone stares at a tire lying on the table.
A cinema wants an ad to “bring people back from their couches.” Half the team admits they haven’t been to the movies in five years.
left: Take the team to a movie

text: The dry-cleaning client is back: “The stains in the ad are too realistic, people are scared.” The stains were drawn.
right: Explain the stains are the point

text: A window manufacturer wants comparison ads: “Our windows beat theirs.” Naming competitors isn’t allowed.
A small local museum asks for an ad on a token budget. It’s the most interesting brief of the year.
Mid-meeting the client announces his company is changing its name. The new name is a secret. The ad is due Friday.
A bathroom fixtures brand wants an ad “like a luxury magazine.” The star is a toilet. The photographer is hunting for “the right light.”
At the review the client can’t pick between two options and suggests “merging them.” One is minimalism, the other a circus.
8 p.m. The owner of a kebab chain sends a voice note: he’s thought of a slogan but won’t share until you offer yours. A contest, he says.
An agribusiness sends an evening brief: “Make young people love potatoes.” Tonight’s dinner happens to be potatoes.
A bridal salon ordered an ad. In the evening the owner sends a reference: her own 40-minute wedding video. She wants “the same, but 30 seconds.”
An old friend opened a café and wants an ad “as a favor.” The agency doesn’t know, and this is your third evening sketching his logo.
right: Keep doing it secretly at night

text: A client you’ve served for five years writes in the evening: “We’ve decided to try another agency. Nothing personal.” A minute later: “Kidding.”
The pizzeria client sends the team twenty pizzas “for a great ad.” The ad isn’t out yet.
right: Give the pizzas to the office next door

text: In the evening the developer asks to rename the housing complex in the ads: “Quiet Harbor” is taken. He suggests “Quiet Harbor 2.”
left: Come up with a new name

text: The coffee shop client writes at 10 p.m.: “Customers say the ad is too good and the coffee is ordinary. Can you make the ad worse?”
A fashion brand wants a shoot “on the streets of the city at night.” It’s 11 p.m., November, drizzling. The models are in summer dresses.
right: Move it to a warm studio

text: In the evening the client sends a competitor’s ad: “Why is theirs better?” The competitor’s budget is twenty times bigger.
right: Write an analysis and a plan

text: A small bookstore asks for an ad and offers to pay in books. Your bookshelf at home already won’t close.
At an evening meeting the client suddenly says: “You know, your team is the only one that gets us.” Then he asks for a discount.
left: Give the discount for the kind words

text: A toy maker sends samples for the shoot. At home, your child demands to keep one. The samples are signed for.
left: Explain the rules to your kid

text: In the evening the client sends “the final edit.” The subject line reads: “Final edit (7).”
right: Suggest a call about all edits

text: A real estate agency wants a “cinematic” ad. In the evening you look at their apartment photos and realize they were shot in the dark on an old phone.
A logistics company wants an ad about “reliability.” In the evening you find out they lost your printed samples.
Late in the evening the owner of a car-repair chain invites you to “discuss the ad informally” in his garage. You’re dreaming of your couch.
A circus ordered an ad for its new show. You’re invited to the dress rehearsal tonight “to feel it.” Early meeting tomorrow.
At 11 p.m. the client sends a photo of his logo embroidered on a pillow. Caption: “I want the ad to feel this cozy.”
right: Reply in the morning with questions

text: In the evening a supermarket chain wants 300 price tags with “emotional” captions by morning. A tag fits four words.
left: Write all night as a team

text: The agency swapped chairs for beanbags “for creativity.” You sit with a laptop on your knees and feel your back handing in its resignation.
A neon sign saying “Be Bold” was hung above your desk. It buzzes and flickers. Especially when you try to focus.
The agency HR asks everyone to write a “value of the month” on a sticky note for the fridge. The fridge is already fully covered.
A new art director joins the team. On day one he declares everything you did last year “visually outdated.”
The office plant you’ve watered for six months turns out to be fake. You found out when it started to smell like a swamp.
left: Laugh and buy a real one
right: Quietly bin it and say nothing

text: You end up in the elevator with the agency head. You have 40 seconds: pitch your idea, or mention the team needs time off.
right: Bring up the team’s time off

text: Morning ping-pong tournament at the agency. The head is playing and clearly wants to win. You’re facing him in the final.
The agency’s new producer built a project schedule: a 400-column spreadsheet color-coded in a way only he understands.
Seating shuffle: you’re placed between the sales team, constantly on calls, and a motion designer who constantly sighs.
You’re interviewing a junior designer. His portfolio is your agency’s work redone “to show how it could be better.”
The agency introduced “Friday demos”: everyone shows what they did this week. Your week went on emails with one client.
left: Present the emails as a case

text: The intern asks how to become a creative director. You have ten minutes before a meeting and, honestly, no answer.
New rule at the agency entrance: bikes in the courtyard only. Your bike is your pride and joy, and someone’s was stolen there yesterday.
The agency head invented a tradition: every Monday morning everyone recites the agency mission in unison. It’s half a page long.
The account manager brought cake to celebrate leaving for another agency. She handled your toughest client. There was no handover.
There’s a fridge war in the office kitchen: someone has kept a prop cake from a shoot there for three weeks. It’s styrofoam, but looks real.
The agency landed a big conservative client. You’re asked to dress “properly” for the meeting. Your most proper outfit is a plain hoodie.
left: Buy a blazer on the way

text: The creative director wants everyone to start a personal blog “for the agency brand.” Your last post was seven years ago.
The producer and creative director fight over the shoot cost. The producer says “unrealistic,” the director says “inspired.” It’s your call.
The agency paid for your online storytelling course. Classes are during work hours, and you have three deadlines this week.
left: Watch the course in the evenings

text: The agency’s new sales manager promises clients “everything in a week.” The creatives already use his photo as a dartboard backdrop.
left: Have a kind chat with him

text: The meeting about reducing meetings is in its third hour. You’re asked to prepare the summary for the next meeting.
The agency’s team-building event is an escape room called “Escape the Deadline.” Meanwhile you have a real deadline you can’t escape.
The rookie copywriter’s text ends every sentence with an exclamation mark. Even the questions!
The retoucher wants a separate dark room: “The sun throws off my color perception.” The only free space is the old props storeroom.
The agency head offers you a new unit — in-game advertising. You haven’t played a game since childhood.
A colleague from the next department keeps “borrowing for a minute” your special presentation marker. He’s had it for a week.
Your creative pair asks to work from the park: “There’s no oxygen for ideas in the office.” The client arrives at 3 p.m.
left: Let them go to the park
right: Ask them to stay until the meeting

text: HR runs an anonymous satisfaction survey. Question 12: “How happy are you, 1 to 10?” Anonymity is ensured by a signature at the bottom.
right: Put an 8 and play it safe

text: Two designers are fighting over a mouse. Literally: there’s one free wireless mouse in the office, and both claim it.
The agency’s key decisions somehow get made by the front door during breaks. You never go there and always find out last.
right: Ask for decisions in the chat

text: You’ve been made mentor to two interns. Both only want to draw characters and refuse to touch layouts.
The office manager asks the creatives to decorate the holiday tree in agency style. The head wants “conceptual,” the team wants “just pretty.”
In the evening the head calls you in: “A rival is poaching you. We know. Let’s talk.” This is news to you.
right: Seize the moment, ask for a raise

text: The agency turns ten. There’s an office party, and you have a delivery in the morning. Everyone wants you for at least one toast.
left: Pop in for half an hour

text: You’re the last person in the office again. The guard knows you by name and asks if you need a blanket.
In the evening the intern confesses he wants to quit advertising to become a pastry chef: “At least nobody asks you to redraw a cake.”
At the evening party you’re asked to perform a number for the creative department. You prepared nothing, and the department already went home.
The agency head proposes a “flexible schedule” in the evening. By his definition: work from nine to infinity.
The agency is doing Secret Santa. You drew the creative director, who “has everything.” The budget covers a chocolate bar.
Your annual review arrives in the evening: “Creative, but not proactive enough.” You wonder how to be more proactive at 2 a.m.
In the evening the team creates a “no work chat” — just memes and cats. An hour later they’re discussing edits in it.
The agency is moving. In the evening you’re asked to pack up the creative department: 400 mock-ups, three mannequins and a stuffed owl.
A colleague spends the evening complaining to you about a client — who is actually your client. He doesn’t know you handle them.
A colleague goes on vacation, leaving you “a few small things.” In the evening you open the list: 14 projects and his email password.
right: Go through it with your manager

text: In the evening the producer says he was a creative himself twenty years ago and “burned bright too.” He offers to teach you “not to burn out.”
The agency head texts at 10 p.m.: “You’re the best. I’ll explain everything tomorrow.” Your heart pounds; sleep is impossible.
right: Turn off the phone and sleep

text: The agency set up a photo spot at the entrance: a giant sign reading “Ideas Are Born Here.” Clients pose there, and you can’t get to your desk.
right: Ask to move the photo spot

text: The agency is launching a podcast. You’re recorded for episode one tonight, but in the “studio” — an old meeting room — you can hear someone frying cutlets.
In the evening you find a note from the cleaner on your desk: “There are 47 sticky notes on your monitor. May I wipe at least half?”
right: Ask her not to touch them

text: The client writes in the morning: “Can the layout ‘pop’? Not literally. Well, literally works too.” It’s an insurance company ad.
Edit of the day: “Make it more modern.” Asked how, the client says: “You know, how they do it now.” He attaches an example — an ad from ten years ago.
The client wants a QR code, phone number, website, office address and directions on the banner. The banner is for an elevator screen.
The layout must be approved by a twelve-person client committee. Twelve emails arrive: eleven “yes” and one “it’s all bad” from the boss.
The client clarifies his edit: “Move everything a tiny bit left. No, not that much. Put it back, but so it feels more left.”
right: Invite him to a joint session

text: Focus group results: everyone liked the ad, but nobody remembered what it was for. Two people think it’s juice. It’s a bank.
The client wants the product photo to look “happier.” The product is a concrete mixer.
The morning edits arrive as a sketch on a café napkin. It looks like a cat. Or a sales chart.
The client’s marketing director wants “more premium feel.” The shoot budget just shrank. Premium, apparently, should be free.
The client writes: “Make the ‘Buy’ button louder.” You look — it’s already red, blinking and half the screen.
left: Add a sound to the button

text: The client wants five languages on one banner “because of our international ambitions.” It’s for a bus stop in a residential suburb.
right: Suggest one language and a website

text: The client writes at 8:00: “Approved yesterday, looked again with fresh eyes — don’t like it. Can’t say why.” Launch in three days.
right: Ask him to compare with the old one

text: The client wants the model replaced: “She’s too beautiful, customers won’t buy it.” The model is an ordinary employee of the client.
Morning edit: “Remove the gradient.” There is no gradient in the layout. He insists he can see it.
The client’s CEO sees the layout for the first time at final approval and asks: “Who came up with this?” His tone is unreadable.
right: Say it was the whole team

text: The client wants the voice-over changed: “Make him sound like me, but better.” He recorded a sample on his phone.
The client at a meeting: “I like it, but let’s show my wife, my mom and my driver. If they all like it, we launch.”
left: Prep a version for the “focus group”

text: The client wants his cat on the banner: “He’s our mascot.” The cat looks displeased. The banner is for a law firm.
left: Use the cat with a caption
right: Talk him into using it on social media

text: The client approved the video, then sent a voice note: “Can everyone dance at the end?” It’s a life insurance ad.
The client asks to make the logo smaller. You read it three times — yes, smaller. The team suspects a trap.
At the review the client says: “The color is fine, but I don’t like its mood.” It’s orange — their brand color.
The client wants the ad to appeal to “everyone from 6 to 90.” The product’s target audience is teenagers.
The client wants the slogan “shorter.” It’s two words. He wants one.
The client sends an edit: “Add more people, but don’t make it crowded.” There are already 40 people in a small kitchen.
The client asks for “a bit of humor, but serious.” Your copywriter slowly closes his laptop.
right: Show examples and agree on it

text: The client approved the layout but needs “a small formality”: signatures from three deputies. One’s on vacation, one’s off sick, one just quit.
On a call the client looks at the layout in silence for two minutes. Then: “Hm.” Nothing else.
right: Wait for him to go on

text: Research shows the audience hates the word “innovative.” The client wants it in the slogan because “we really are innovative.”
The client wants “the same as last time, only different.” Last time was two years ago, and he didn’t like it then either.
At the review the client asks: “Why is there a dog?” It’s an ad for dog food.
right: Offer a version with a cat

text: The client wants the music changed to “something emotional but without emotion.” The composer replies with 30 seconds of silence.
right: Ask the composer to try again

text: The client wants a “sense of presence” in the apartment ad. Your 3D visualizer asks whether he means “the smell of fresh paint.”
9 p.m. The client sends “final final” edits and adds: “Not urgent.” Ten minutes later: “So, when?”
In the evening the client sends edits to a layout you haven’t shown him. He found it on the agency site under “coming soon.”
In the evening the client says he’s changed his mind about the whole concept. Reason: he dreamed the ad flopped.
Before bed the client writes: “In the morning please send a version with all edits except the ones I cancelled.” Which ones he cancelled is unclear.
right: Ask for the list in the morning

text: In the evening the client finds an error on a banner that’s been up for a month. It’s a comma. He demands all billboards be reprinted.
right: Fix it in the next print run

text: Late at night the client sends his own storyboard: “I sketched how it should be.” It’s drawn in pen on a receipt.
At 10:30 p.m. the client posts: “Awake? It occurred to me the logo looks sad.” The logo is a smiling sun.
right: Reply in the morning with a smile

text: In the evening the client sends a link to an ad he “saw yesterday and loved.” It’s your ad, for another client.
right: Stay quiet and do something similar

text: In the evening the client drops a week of his own edits and asks for the original version. Naturally, nobody saved it.
In the evening the client writes: “Looked at all 12 options, I pick number 13.” There was no 13.
Late in the evening the client wants the ad to show “me, but young.” The only old photo shows him in a bunny costume.
In the evening the client asks to change autumn to spring in the video. It’s edited and graded; the trees are yellow.
In the evening the client writes: “Great job, no edits!” You read it twice in disbelief. An hour later: “One tiny one.”
right: Ask him to wait till morning

text: The client wants the video reworked into vertical format. It was shot horizontally, with the hero and product at opposite edges.
In the evening the client sends a voice note cheerfully singing your jingle. He asks to “put it in like this” — off-key, but heartfelt.
right: Praise him and keep the singer

text: The client’s lawyer strikes “best” from the slogan, then “most,” then “tasty.” Of “The Tastiest Is the Best,” only the dash remains.
The layout goes to the client’s board. Each of the seven directors asks to change one element. The layout has five elements.
left: Make a version with seven edits

text: The client’s manager writes that the boss is “generally pleased” but wants to “play with fonts a little more.” You’ve been playing with fonts for three weeks.
right: Offer a final pick of two

text: In the morning your kid asks for help with a school project: “Draw a logo for our class.” The teacher wants it by 8:30; you have a call at 8:45.
right: Help, but let the kid draw

text: You’re working from home. Morning client call, and the neighbor starts renovating. The drill hits every pause.
left: Take the call from the car

text: Your cat walked across the keyboard and sent the client “ffffffffzzzz.” The client replied: “Agreed.”
At morning drop-off the daycare teacher finds out you work in advertising and asks for a “Our Autumn” wall newspaper by lunch.
For the first time in a month you’re having breakfast at home without staring at your phone. It’s on the table, buzzing nonstop.
Your neighbor recognized your ad at the bus stop and asks you to “neighborly” design a sign for her nail salon.
Your kids are arguing over whose turn it is to watch cartoons. You suggest a “pitch”: whoever makes the best case wins.
Your car won’t start. Pitch in an hour, no taxis — it’s snowing. A neighbor offers a ride on his tractor.
At breakfast your partner looks at your layout and says: “I don’t get what’s being sold.” You present it in two hours.
Your dog wakes you at 5:30 for a walk. You went to bed at 2:00 after edits. The walk is inevitable; the question is how long.
left: Long walk and wake up properly
right: Quick loop and back to bed

text: Grandma calls in the morning and asks you to explain “what exactly you do.” Last time it took forty minutes.
You try a coworking space “for a change of scene.” The guy next to you is loudly discussing your own tender on the phone.
The mail carrier brings a parcel to your home: the client’s product samples. Forty kilos of cat litter. You live on the fifth floor, no elevator.
right: Ask to have it sent to the office

text: Your kid’s teacher invites you to talk about your job in class. The class is at 9:00 on the day of a big presentation.
On the bus, schoolkids are discussing your ad: “Somebody thought this was funny.” You hold the rail and learn the truth about your audience.
The agency head wants everyone working remotely to keep cameras on all day “for team spirit.” Your home is mid-renovation chaos.
Your back has hurt for three days thanks to the office beanbag. The only doctor slots are on a weekday morning.
During a client call your kid walks into frame in a dinosaur costume and roars. The client goes quiet.
Your parents drop by in the middle of your work-from-home day. Mom starts vacuuming during your call with the production company.
The neighbor next door holds his remote calls so loudly you now know all his projects. Today he’s discussing your agency.
You’re cooking lunch at home when the client video-calls “for two minutes.” Twenty minutes later your cutlet is burning and he’s just getting started.
The courier delivered your lunch to the client’s address because you mistyped the app. The client sends a photo: “Is this a hint?”
Your kid asks for help with drawing homework while you’re stuck on a client concept. His drawing unexpectedly gives you the idea.
left: Credit the kid and say thanks

text: Your partner calls in the afternoon asking if you’ll make family dinner at 7. You have a “short” client meeting at 6.
During an online brainstorm your parrot starts squawking “Great! Great!” after every idea. The team laughs; the creative director, less so.
The class parents’ chat asks you, “as a professional,” to design T-shirts for the school event. Forty parents are sending suggestions.
A friend invites you to lunch, but you’re thinking about the deadline. She says all you’ve talked about for a month is logos.
Your home internet dies five minutes before your presentation. The nearest Wi-Fi is the café around the corner with loud music.
A relative calls with a “genius ad idea” — a song about her vegetable garden. She already recorded a verse.
While you were at work your partner painted a wall in “your signature color,” from the ad. It’s an awful color.
right: Praise it and get used to it

text: Your friends ask in the group chat why you missed a third birthday in a row. You were at a shoot, a pitch and an edit session.
left: Promise to make the next one

text: Your boss writes: “Why aren’t you online?” You just stepped out to a shop for ten minutes after eight hours without a break.
At lunch you’re cycling to a client with paper layouts in your backpack. A downpour starts.
At the shoot the client brings his hamster: “He has to be in it, he’s our mascot.” The hamster is asleep.
You come home and everyone expects you to “come up with how to celebrate the anniversary.” You spent all day coming up with things for others.
Your partner asks for a phone-free evening. At 9 p.m. a client message arrives marked “very urgent.”
