At bedtime your kid asks for a story. You find yourself telling one about “a mascot who wanted to be bigger than the logo.”
right: Ask the kid to invent the ending

text: At family dinner you’re asked not to talk about work. Five minutes later you’re telling them about the client who wanted to “remove the happiness from the photo.”
In the evening the neighbor knocks and asks you to print twenty notices about a tenants’ meeting. He knows you “have a printer in advertising.”
The evening news runs a piece on “ads that annoy everyone.” Exhibit A: your video. Your family turns to look at you.
You’re finally in the bath with a book, and a campaign idea hits. The notebook is in another room; your hands are wet.
In the evening friends argue about who makes ads. One is sure “AI does it all.” You take a deep breath.
Your parents send a video: they recreated your ad’s dance in the courtyard. The neighbors joined in.
left: Forward it to the team chat
right: Ask them not to post it online

text: You sit down to watch a series. Every five minutes you catch yourself thinking “who designed these titles?” You can’t relax.
Home is chaos: laundry, dinner, homework with your kid. Then a client email: “just take a quick look at one file.”
You’re on vacation by the sea. An evening email from the agency: “Not bothering you, you’re just cc’d.” You’ve been cc’d forty times.
You signed up for evening swimming. Today the client set a “quick call” for 7 p.m. The pass will expire.
In the evening the cat sits squarely on the layout on your desk and refuses to move. As far as he’s concerned, it’s approved.
You go to bed at 10 p.m. for the first time in a month. Five minutes later you remember you didn’t send the client the final file.
Your partner asks for help with a presentation for work: “You know how, make it pretty.” It’s 60 slides about logistics.
right: Teach the basics in an hour

text: The new business director announces the agency is in four tenders at once. Same deadlines. Same team.
The client invites agencies to a “chemistry meeting.” You’re asked to share something unusual about yourself.
The tender rules say: “Creative concept — two pages max. Font size 14 minimum.” Your concept is six pages.
The agency credentials deck is three years old. It still features an employee who left and an office you moved out of.
The creative director wants the whole team to enter the pitch dressed as the product. The product is squash caviar.
You learn your rival in the tender is the agency where your former mentor works. He texts: “Good luck. You’ll need it.”
The morning of the pitch the client sends a “small addition” to the brief: the product is now for retirees, not kids.
The client wants printed decks “for each attendee.” According to them, there’ll be “between five and forty.”
right: Print ten and send a file

text: The intern asks if he can come to the pitch “just to watch.” He promises to stay quiet. You know he can’t.
The tender portal freezes 20 minutes before the deadline. Your file is 87% uploaded.
An agency partner says “making an impression” at the pitch is key and suggests renting a live swan. The pitch budget is zero.
left: Talk him out of the swan

text: The client warns the pitch will be “just 15 minutes, including questions.” You have 60 slides and a 4-minute video.
left: Keep the video and three slides

text: Morning pitch run-through. The creative director asks you to play a “skeptical client” and ask tough questions. You’re a little too good at it.
At the pitch it turns out you must present from the client’s laptop. Your deck won’t open on it, and your fonts are missing.
The new business director sends you a list of “hot” prospects. Half of them are already your agency’s clients.
Right before the pitch you realize the pricing slide shows another client’s prices. The creative director has the clicker.
The agency head suggests rehearsing the pitch over breakfast in a café. Five minutes in, you spot the client’s staff at the next table.
At the pitch the client says: “We love it. Can we take these ideas and give them to our in-house team?” He is dead serious.
The client says they’ll choose between you and the rival “by lot,” since “both are equally good.”
After the pitch the client asks you to “develop the idea a bit” before deciding. “A bit” means the full campaign. For free.
You lost the tender. The client’s feedback is one word: “Decent.” The team wants to know what went wrong.
During the pitch the client’s vice president falls asleep. The others glance at him, unsure whether to continue.
Procurement asks you to submit the creative director’s hourly rate. The creative director believes his time is priceless.
At the pitch the client suddenly asks to see the idea you rejected. It exists only on the copywriter’s napkin.
During the pitch the creative director improvises and promises the client “an ad on the Moon.” The client is writing it down.
The tender demands “three concepts, two videos and a media plan” in five working days. The prize: “experience and portfolio.”
After the pitch the client wants the deck “in an editable format to show management.” You suspect it’ll be shown without your logo.
You won the tender! The client says the first project is needed “this week.” The team just took days off after the pitch.
After the pitch you run into the rival team in the hallway. They suggest coffee to “compare notes.”
The client’s tender office says your bid was rejected because the director signed in the wrong box.
After your pitch the client asks: “Can you do the same thing for a third of the price?” The team sits stone-faced.
The client announces the tender results: everyone won, and each agency gets a small slice of the project.
11 p.m., tender due tomorrow. The creative director decides to change the whole idea. He’ll explain the new one “as we go.”
The evening after the pitch the client calls to say they “really liked you personally.” The agency hasn’t been chosen yet.
In the evening the new business director says a prospect wants you at a pitch tomorrow at 8 a.m., in another city.
After losing the tender the team gathers in the office. Nobody wants to leave. Someone suggests pizza and a post-mortem.
An evening email: “You won the tender. But our director changed, so we’re rerunning it.”
The night before the pitch the deck is 2 GB and won’t go by email. The client asks you to “just send the file.”
Late in the evening the client accidentally posts the budget he expects in the tender group chat. It’s half your estimate.
After the pitch the creative director writes: “We were brilliant. If we don’t win, the client just isn’t ready for us.”
In the evening you realize there’s no proper final slide for tomorrow. The last slide is “Thank you for your attention” in the default font.
right: End with a strong line out loud

text: The agency head gathers everyone in the evening: “We lost the tender, but I’m proud of you.” Then announces a new tender tomorrow.
left: Thank him and go to sleep

text: In the evening after the pitch you see the client liked the rival agency’s post. The team is anxious.
The night before the tender the printer only prints every other page. Submission must be on paper, in two copies.
left: Print one page at a time

text: You won the tender, and in the evening the new client sends a 12-page welcome letter. Last line: “Looking forward to first results tomorrow.”
right: Reply with thanks and a timeline

text: In the evening you decide to pull out of a tender where your work would clearly end up free. The agency head doesn’t know yet.
You’re waiting to pitch in the client’s meeting room. Left on the whiteboard: “Agency B — expensive, Agency C — boring.” You’re Agency C.
left: Snap a photo of the board

text: At the pitch the client asks you to “act out” the ad live, no video. The creative director looks at you: you did school drama club.
The night before the pitch you lose your voice. You’re the lead presenter. Tea with honey isn’t helping.
In the evening the courier is supposed to deliver the tender box to the client. He calls: “The box got soaked, I got caught in the rain.”
7 a.m., the expo center. The client’s stand opens at 10, but the installers built it backwards: the logo faces the wall.
right: Hang a second logo on the other side

text: The promo staff for the yogurt tasting didn’t show. Only one came, dressed as a giant yogurt. The costume fits one.
The branded T-shirts arrived this morning. The brand name is misspelled on every one. The event is in three hours.
The outdoor installers call at 6 a.m.: they can’t hang the facade banner — too windy. The client arrives to photograph it at 9.
The host of the product launch is sick. The client suggests you host: “You came up with it all, you tell it.” Starts at 11.
The agency ordered gift bags for event guests. Instead of branded notebooks, they contain another brand’s notebooks.
right: Pull the notebooks from every bag

text: The venue for a new soda flavor launch is booked for a wedding. The manager mixed up the dates. Guests for both events are on their way.
The mascot costume arrives at the agency. It’s unsettling: the eyes look in different directions, and the smile is far too wide.
right: Make it a social media star

text: The printer calls at 8: the flyers are done, but the color “drifted a bit green.” They’re for a coffee chain, to be handed out today.
At the client’s store opening, the photo spot has giant letters. One fell, so “Cozy Home” now reads “Cozy Hom.” Guests are already posing.
right: Rush to put the letter back

text: The caterer at a bank’s launch brought canapés shaped like a competitor’s logo. A coincidence, but very noticeable.
right: Joke about it in the speech

text: The event sound engineer mixed up the playlist: instead of a grand entrance theme, the CEO walks out to a children’s song.
Your ad installation — a giant coffee cup — went up in the park. This morning it turns out pigeons are sleeping in it.
left: Make the pigeons part of the story

text: The LED screen at the event shows your presentation with a stripe across the middle — right through the speaker’s face on every slide.
The press wall features all sponsor logos. The main sponsor is unhappy: his is the same size as everyone else’s.
left: Print a bigger logo for him

text: At the tasting for the client’s new sauce, it turns out to be very spicy. The first three guests are in tears. The line is growing.
right: Hand out milk with each sample

text: Three times more guests than expected showed up. There’s food for a third. The client is thrilled and wants “even more people next time.”
A mall promo: shoppers have to dance to get a coupon. Only the security guards are dancing. Shoppers are shy.
At the trade show the client’s competitor comes to your stand asking very detailed questions about the campaign. His badge says “Visitor.”
Twenty bloggers were invited to the product launch. Three came and asked for an “appearance fee.” That’s not in the contract.
At the client’s corporate party the host gets your agency’s name wrong. Three times. The client laughs; your head does not.
Your billboard was installed upside down. Photos spread online, and brand awareness doubled in a day.
left: Leave it up for a day

text: At the brand’s kids’ party the mascot entertainer takes off his head for a drink of water. The kids are shocked; parents are filming.
left: Spin it as “the mascot is tired”

text: The client’s director is forty minutes late to his own press conference. Journalists are starting to leave.
The client ordered 5,000 branded pens. They all write in red. The client is a bank.
The curtain on your event stage is stuck. Half the set is visible. The client’s CEO is already walking out.
right: Hold his entrance for a minute

text: The neighboring trade-show stand blasts music at full volume. Your guests can’t hear the client’s presentation. The organizers shrug.
The “Bring an old pan, get a discount on a new one” promo worked too well. The client’s office holds 800 old pans.
left: Turn them into an art piece

text: The event photographer shot all day, but every photo is a close-up of the cake. Almost no people.
A journalist at the event asks how much it cost. The client asked you not to disclose figures. The journalist won’t let go.
The AC is broken at the client’s partner party. It’s sweltering, and guests are fanning themselves with your brochures.
The hired host is reading the wrong script — from another event. He congratulates the guests on “the factory’s anniversary.”
Evening. The event is over, guests have gone, and the client wants a photo report “by morning, for the board.”
Stand teardown at 10 p.m. The installers left you half the structure and instructions in a foreign language.
After the event, 300 balloons with the client’s logo are left over. The venue must be cleared in an hour.
After the event the client calls, thrilled: “Let’s do it again next week, but twice as big!”
right: Ask for a month to prepare

text: You’re taking the mascot costume home because there’s no storage at the agency. The taxi driver refuses to drive with “that.”
11:30 p.m. You’re installing a light display on a building facade. Building security decides you’re thieves and calls the police.
In the evening the event producer sends the final budget. It’s a third over the approved one. The line “unforeseen balloons” is especially impressive.
left: Go through it line by line
right: Send it to the client as is

text: After a 16-hour event the team is sitting on the venue floor. Someone suggests eating the leftover cake with their hands.
In the evening you find a clip of your mascot falling off the stage. It’s gaining views faster than the entire campaign.
right: Ask for it to be taken down

text: The agency wants last year’s event props cleared out of storage by morning. There are five crates labeled “DO NOT OPEN.”
Late in the evening the client sends an event photo where your eyes are closed. He wants it as the lead image in the press release.
After the trade show you end up with 50 of the client’s branded mugs at home. Your family is already drinking tea from them and wants more.
An event you organized has been nominated for an award. In the evening you learn a rival agency entered it as their own.
right: Let it go and move on

text: The night before the campaign launch. You check everything for the tenth time. It all works. That’s scarier than if something broke.
The brand’s evening show. The pyro tech asks if he can add “a bit more fire.” The venue is a shopping mall rooftop.
10:40 p.m. The venue guard says the rental ended at 10 and every half hour is a fine. The client’s guests are dancing and not leaving.
right: Pay the fine and let them dance

text: The set van driver calls at night: broken down on the highway, no fix until morning. The sets are needed at the venue by 8.
The evening before the event the client sends an “updated” guest list. Two hundred names longer, all “very important.”
The client wants a name for a new cheese. All 200 names you suggested are already trademarked. Even “Cheesy McCheeseface.”
right: Suggest a name with a number

text: The copywriter brings in copy using the word “unique” 14 times. He says it’s “an amplification technique.”
right: Keep it as a stylistic device

text: The client wants packaging where “everything is obvious at once”: pasta, a plate, a fork, a pot and a stove on the pasta box.
This morning you came up with a laundromat slogan: “A clean conscience from 199.” The creative director loves it; the lawyer doesn’t.
In the morning you find the client’s brand account posted something unscheduled overnight: “Test test test.” 300 likes.
right: Play it up in the next post

text: The client wants a 300-page brand book, “like the big guys.” His company is a single kebab stand by the train station.
You notice a missing letter in the slogan on every city bus. “Ride Together” now reads “Ride Togther.” The buses are already running.
The client’s new brand manager decided a baby food brand should sound “sassy, like a teenager.” Moms in the comments aren’t impressed.
The team named a flower delivery app “Posy.” This morning it turns out that’s the name of a dating app.
The copywriter admits he writes his best copy only on trains. There are no trains in town, only a tram.
left: Send him to ride the tram
right: Ask him to write at his desk

text: Under the dumpling brand’s post someone asks: “What exactly are your dumplings made of?” The brief has no answer.
The client wants a slogan “for the ages” — remembered a hundred years from now. Deadline: lunch.
right: Propose a slogan for one year

text: The agency proofreader is off for a month. During that month a 200-page catalog comes out. You only spot your typos once they’re printed.
The client sent back the script: “Too many words.” The script has one word — the brand name.
The client wants every social media comment answered within five minutes. Two hundred comments an hour, and you’re alone on the account.
This morning the art director pitched a slogan and the copywriter a visual. They’ve apparently swapped roles and are happy.
right: Put them back in their lanes

text: The client suggests a deliberate typo in the slogan: “So everyone talks about it.” You fear they’ll talk about the brand’s spelling.
A customer filmed the client’s product breaking in his hands. The video is spreading. The client wants “something done, now.”
The client picked a name for a new drink. You check: in one language it means “old sock.” The product is for export.
right: Stay quiet, maybe no one notices

text: The copywriter refuses to write “sales copy”: “I’m a poet.” He wrote a sonnet about laundry detergent. It’s beautiful.
left: Pitch the sonnet to the client

text: The brand account you run has been dragged into a spat with another brand. Followers want a reply. The client is on a plane.
The printer sent a packaging proof. It’s lovely, but the barcode is right across the mascot’s face. Reprinting takes a week.
The client wants a press release about his “anniversary”: the company turned three years and two months old.
Hundreds of comments under the brand’s post are from one person. He hates the packaging color and posts about it every five minutes.
The client brings a slogan his driver came up with: “Near when you’re far.” It fits perfectly; your thirty don’t.
Someone found a mistake: the ad shows a city where the client has no stores. Locals are asking where the store is.
left: Suggest the client open one there

text: The client wants you to “tell the brand story.” The story: the founder thought for a long time, then opened a store. That’s it.
Your slogan must be adapted for five countries. Every translator suggests changes that leave nothing of the original.
The client wants 30 hashtags in every post “for reach.” The post is a cat photo with a three-word caption.
right: Show data that it doesn’t work

text: The copywriter delivers 8,000 characters of copy for a billboard. A billboard fits seven words.
You accidentally sent the client’s promo email not to 500 subscribers but to the whole database — 200,000 addresses, including unsubscribers.
The editor wants to add a “goosebumps effect” — slow music and close-ups. The ad is for cockroach spray.
The client wants the copy rewritten “for simpler people.” An hour later, “for smarter people.” An hour after that, “for everyone.”
The creative team voted on a product name. The winner: “Fluffy.” The product is industrial glue.
9 p.m. An argument erupts under the brand’s post about whether the slogan’s comma is correct. It’s getting personal.
In the evening a popular blogger criticizes the client’s ad. The client asks you to write him “a harsh reply.”
At 10 p.m. the copywriter sends the final copy: “Don’t read it, just send it.” You read it — he got the brand name wrong.
In the evening the client sends an “updated brand book” with a new brand color. All campaign materials are printed in the old one.
At 11 p.m. you realize the brand you run is supposed to congratulate followers on a holiday. The post isn’t ready, and the holiday is today.
Just before sleep the perfect product name pops into your head. You’ll forget it by morning. The notebook is in the hallway.
left: Get up and write it down

text: In the evening the client learns his slogan matches a line from a children’s song. People are already singing it in the comments.
In the evening an elderly man messages the support chat of the brand you run: he just wants to talk. It’s been forty minutes.
Late in the evening the copywriter asks if you’d like to read his novel. 600 pages. He says you’re the first reader.
right: Honestly say you don’t have time

text: After sending the newsletter you notice the subject line says “{NAME}” instead of the customer’s name. Recipients are already replying.
right: Joke about it in the next one

text: In the evening a review appears on the client’s site: “The ad is better than the product.” The client asks whether that’s good or bad.
Overnight your brand account won a spat with another brand with a witty reply. In the morning the client will ask who approved it.
Late in the evening the creative director posts a poll: “Which slogan is better, 1 or 2?” They’re identical except for a period.
In the evening the client wants captions for 120 catalog photos. Every photo is the same: a white mug on a white background.
11:20 p.m. Doing one last read of the brochure, you find “Holiday Sael” in the headline. The printer closed at 11.
In a copywriters’ group chat someone asks for advice: a client insists on “We’re number one,” though they’re number seven. Everyone wants your take.
In the morning the agency head offers to make you creative director. The condition: you no longer make things yourself, only “guide.”
Updating your portfolio, you realize your best work never ran — clients rejected it. What’s left are compromises.
You’ve been invited to speak at an ad conference. The suggested topic: “How Not to Burn Out.” You’re writing it at 6 a.m. after a night shift.
A big network agency wants to buy yours. The head gathers everyone: “Nothing will change.” Everyone knows everything will.
You’ve been invited to judge a student ad competition. 300 entries by Friday. Your projects haven’t gone anywhere.
A headhunter writes: a rival agency offers more money. But rumor has it everyone works nights there, including the cleaner.
Your junior designer asks why his layout wasn’t picked but yours — “almost the same” — was. He’s right, they’re nearly identical.
right: Pitch his version to the client

text: The agency head asks you to write a bio for the agency site, “something creative.” Everyone else wrote: “I love cats and coffee.”
You teach an ad course on Saturdays. A student sends homework better than what you made yesterday.
left: Praise it and learn from it

text: Your new assistant tries too hard: by 7 a.m. he’s sent you 14 emails with ideas, plans and questions.
After the agencies merged you have two creative directors who give opposite instructions. Today both are in the same meeting.
left: Ask them to agree between themselves

text: The new creative director begins by banning the word “fine.” From now on, it’s either “fire” or “redo.”
A former client sends a thank-you note: your ad from five years ago still brings him customers.
Your intern messages every morning: “What should I do today?” You don’t have an answer even for yourself.
A former colleague who moved to client-side marketing is now your client. He remembers all your jokes about clients.
A trade publication ranks creatives. You’re 47th, right behind an intern from a rival agency.
You go to ask the head for a raise. Three colleagues are already waiting with the same request and folders of achievements.
The creative director entered your work for an award, listing himself as lead author. Your name is fifth of five.
You’re asked to run a workshop for clients on “creative thinking.” In an hour. No slides.
Your former mentor asks for help with an idea for his new agency. It’s your direct rival in the current tender.
You’re offered a client-side job in a big company’s marketing. More money, fewer nights, less creativity.
A junior comes to you in tears: the client called his layout “a child’s drawing.” It was his first review.
The studio whose ads you idolized as a teenager reaches out. They offer a weekend test assignment.
The agency is rebranding to something “more modern.” The suggestion: “Creative Hub Lab.” You’re tasked with explaining it to clients.
A trade publication runs a piece on your project, but only the agency head is mentioned. You’re not in it.
left: Ask them to add the credit

text: At a partners’ meeting they’re picking a head for a new unit. You were invited “for objectivity.” You’re also on the shortlist.
You’re taking two weeks off for the first time in a year. The head says: “Of course! Just stay reachable.” Clients are already asking “who’s covering.”
Your team asks you to stand up for them: they got no bonus for winning the tender. The head says “that was their job.”
The client offers you a staff job: “You’ll do our ads without an agency.” The agency head doesn’t know.
You receive the agency’s “Employee of the Month.” The prize: a parking spot. You don’t have a car.
The agency sends you to a “Client Communication” training. The trainer is the former client who rejected your layout last week.
The art director announces he’s leaving. As a parting gift he wants to redo your best joint project “the way he always wanted.”
After your talk at the conference a student tells you he went into advertising because of your ad.
An official job offer from a rival arrives in the evening. A third more pay. Tomorrow you have a stand-up with your team.
In the evening the creative director confides he’s leaving and has recommended you as his replacement. The agency head isn’t sold yet.
In the evening you work on a personal project — a comic. Your agency contract says “all employee ideas belong to the agency.”
At the farewell party for a colleague moving to another agency, you’re asked to give a toast. You argued with her about every font for three years.
Your former intern sends a photo: he won his first award. He says he couldn’t have done it without you.
right: Ask him to speak at your agency

text: In the evening you list pros and cons of leaving the agency. The pros list is longer, but the cons include your team.
right: Leave, but help with the handover

text: An industry meetup for creatives this evening. You hate networking, but people you’d love to work with will be there.
In the evening you get anonymous team feedback: “Good lead, but sometimes messages at midnight.” You’re reading it at 11:55 p.m.
right: Reply to the team in the morning

text: After the merger you’re told in the evening that your role is being “combined” with a counterpart from the other agency. Decision in a week.
In the evening the agency head asks where you see yourself in five years. Honestly, you don’t know where you’ll be tomorrow.
Late at night you dig up the first ad you made ten years ago. It’s terrible. But it has a boldness you’ve lost.
You’re invited to judge an international award. 800 entries over two weeks of evenings.
In the evening the intern asks whether he can stay after his internship. It’s not your call, but he looks at you hopefully.
left: Promise to put in a word
right: Say honestly it’s not up to you

text: A publisher asks you to write a book about advertising. Six months, written in evenings and weekends.
In the evening a former client you fell out with a year ago writes: “We were wrong. Let’s work together again.”
In the evening design students ask you to look at their thesis projects “even briefly.” Twelve projects, presentations in two days.
In the evening the agency CFO invites you for “a talk about the future.” Turns out he wants you to teach him to draw.
You arrive at 9 after delivering at 4 a.m. The client has already sent “a couple of observations.” There are nineteen.
right: Nap in the meeting room first

text: The creative director is surprised in the morning: “Why does everyone look so tired?” Yesterday he asked for everything redone by morning.
8:55. The video is due to the client at 9:00. The upload has 12 minutes left. The client is already texting “So?”
After an all-nighter you’re at the coffee machine. A colleague suggests “a double espresso with a double espresso.” Your heart begs for mercy.
In the morning you discover that at 3:47 a.m. you emailed the client: “so yeah, basically, you get it.” No attachment.
Morning. The editor delivered at 5 a.m. and fell asleep on the edit-room couch. The client wants a title changed urgently. Wake him?
The alarm rings at 7. You went to bed at 4. First meeting at 10. You could sleep an hour more and skip the workout you never do anyway.
Your department looks like a battlefield: pizza boxes, printouts on the floor, someone asleep under a desk. A client tour arrives in an hour.
In the morning the client pushes the deadline back a week. You worked all night for today’s.
right: Ask for earlier notice next time

text: The account manager asks brightly: “How was the night? Did you make it?” He left at 6 p.m. yesterday.
You’re riding to work after a sleepless night. The driver recognizes you as “the one behind the singing chicken ad” and plays it on his phone.
Morning client call. You can barely keep your eyes open. Cameras are expected, and you look like a horror movie character.
left: Turn it on and own it

text: The designer arrives saying he spent all night thinking about the project and “finally gets it.” The project was delivered yesterday.
right: Suggest saving it for another project

text: The agency head praises you in front of everyone for working through the night — and suggests “making it a tradition.” The team stares at you.
The printer calls at 7:30: “We got the file overnight. Did you really want the text in Latin?” It was placeholder text.
right: Stop the press and sort it out

text: The intern who stayed overnight with you looks fresher than anyone. He says it was “the best night of his life.”
right: Bring him to the morning meeting

text: You leave the office at 6 a.m. after an overnight render and see the sunrise. Beautiful. You need to be back in three hours.
right: Watch the sunrise in the park

text: After a sleepless night you accidentally call the client by his competitor’s name in a meeting. He freezes.
right: Act like it was on purpose

text: After a night shift you fall asleep at lunch in a café. The waiter gently wakes you and asks if you’re okay.
At the meeting the client says: “We saw the overnight version. Let’s go back to yesterday’s daytime one.” The overnight cost you your sleep.
The account manager promised “tomorrow morning” again. You realize that means another night at the office.
right: Accept it and work through the night

text: You’re so tired you ask an AI to write the client email. It’s very polite but addresses the client as “Dear User.”
You notice that overnight you sent the client the version with a full-screen “DRAFT” watermark. He’s already shown it to his bosses.
right: Send the final with a note

text: A colleague who also pulled an all-nighter asks you to cover for him while he naps in his car. The head is looking for him.
In a meeting after a sleepless night you realize you’ve been nodding for five minutes without listening. The client asks: “Do you agree?”
You ask for a day off after three straight nights. The head says: “Of course, but not today, not tomorrow and not the day after.”
After two all-nighters the team proposes a rule: “No more ‘by morning’ deadlines.” The head asks you to back or veto it.
After the night, the editor mixed up the music: the bank ad has the cat food ad’s soundtrack. It sounds surprisingly good.
left: Keep it and show the client

text: After a week of nights your eye starts twitching. A colleague says “just get some sleep.” The client says “push a little harder.”
left: Take a day off and sleep

text: The well-rested creative director arrives with new ideas. You haven’t slept and only want fewer ideas.
The project is delivered and the client is happy. The head proposes “celebrating” — with a new urgent project he’s “already promised.”
The agency put a couch in the meeting room “for resting.” Now someone’s always asleep there, and there’s nowhere to meet.
right: Leave the couch to the sleepers

text: The animation contractor says he’ll deliver not by morning but “by morning his time.” He’s on another continent — that’s your evening.
2:30 a.m. You and the designer are the last ones in. He says: “You know, I don’t think we’re making it better anymore. Just different.”
The final render will take six hours. Delivery at 8 a.m. It’s 1 a.m. Stay and guard it, or go home and pray.
Midnight. Working on the deck, you realize you last ate at lunch. Delivery at this hour costs as much as a restaurant dinner.
At night the guard walks in and asks if you’re okay. It’s the third night in a row he’s asked.
At 3 a.m. the client replies: “Thanks, will look in the morning.” You realize he can’t sleep either.
At night you discover three people from other projects still in the office. Everyone acts like it’s normal.
At 1 a.m. the creative director sends a voice note: “I was thinking — let’s keep everything as it was.” You redid it all this evening.
Alone in the office at night, you crank the music to stay awake. In the morning you’ll learn the guard filmed you dancing.
11:50 p.m. Ten minutes to the deadline. The file is nearly done, but one detail could be better. That would take an hour.
right: Make it better and be late

text: 4 a.m. The work is delivered. The office is quiet. Go home, or sleep on the couch here and skip the commute.
Your partner calls at midnight: “Are you coming home at all?” You’re not finished, but you promised to be back by ten.
At night the creative director asks in the chat: “Who’s awake?” Answer, and you get a task. Don’t, and you get it in the morning.
You make the last metro train after late work. It’s just you and a cleaner, who looks at your laptop and asks if it’s really that bad.
Late at night you realize tomorrow — well, today — is your birthday. There are three meetings on the calendar.
The night before delivery you realize the campaign’s beloved main idea is actually a bit sad. Nobody noticed.
right: Keep it — sadness is honest too

text: A courier brings food someone on the team ordered overnight “for the morning.” Twelve servings of pancakes. Nobody owns up.
At night the lamp over your desk burns out. You can work by monitor light, but by morning you’ll be seeing colors differently.
The client ordered one banner “in all sizes.” The list has 64 formats, from a skinny vertical strip to a stamp-sized square.
right: Do the top 10 plus a template

text: The ad platform rejected your banner: “Too much text.” The text is one word, just very large.
The client sees the new site and wants the homepage “like a magazine — with page flips.” The site is already built.
right: Explain why it’s a bad idea

text: The analyst ran a test on two banners. Result: identical to a hundredth of a percent. The client wants “a winner.”
The web developer says your design is “impossible to build.” The designer says “anything is possible.” Both look at you.
The client wants a mobile app for his bakery, “like the big brands.” The app would show a menu of six buns.
The client is upset his site isn’t first in search for “best bakery in the world.” He wants an explanation by lunch.
The animated banner is ten times over the size limit. The platform rejects it. The motion designer says it’s “a shame to cut the animation.”
Your billboard stands right behind a tree. In summer it’s invisible. The client noticed in July; the campaign started in April.
left: Move the board at your cost
right: Negotiate a discount with the vendor

text: The client wants a newsletter with video, animation and a mini-game. Most subscribers’ email apps only show plain text.
left: Make a fancy and a plain version

text: The client complains: “On my phone the site is yellow, it should be orange.” He has night mode on.
The promo landing page is due at 10. At 9:40 the client changes the offer: not 20% off but “a pleasant surprise.”
The social video must be vertical, square and horizontal at once. The client wants “everything visible” in each format.
The client wants a chatbot that answers “with the brand’s humor.” The brand is a funeral service.
The client asks why there are lots of clicks but no sales. You check: the “Buy” button on the site leads nowhere.
The ad platform suspended the client’s account for “suspicious activity.” The suspicious activity is you, making edits at 4 a.m.
The client’s site crashes every time your ad runs. The better the ad works, the worse the site does.
The client wants a logo animation “like in movies, where it explodes and reassembles.” Budget: a static image.
Moderation rejected the video because a cucumber is shown “for an unacceptably long time.” It’s a salad ad.
The client’s site shows your beautiful font only on your computer. Everyone else sees the default font.
The targeting specialist wants to show stroller ads only to people “who searched for strollers.” The client wants “everyone who might have kids.”
You bought stock footage of “a happy office team” for the video. A week later you see the same footage in ads for three other brands.
The client opens the site on his phone and his thumb covers the “Buy” button. He thinks it’s missing.
The client brings AI-generated images: “Make it like this.” The people in them have six fingers.
The media planner suggests placing luxury watch ads in a calorie-counting app. “Impressions are super cheap there,” he explains.
The client wants “that annoying music” taken out of the ad. It’s his company anthem, which he commissioned himself.
The client wants phone, address, website and menu on a highway billboard. Drivers see it for two seconds.
The blogger’s integration script: 30 seconds about the brand and nine minutes on his new hobby, baking. The brand sells tires.
right: Ask him to tie it to tires

text: The analyst shows the client’s sales peak matched not your ad but the day a competitor’s store broke down.
The client tests the app prototype and taps everything that isn’t a button. Every five seconds he says: “Doesn’t work.”
The agency website is down: nobody renewed the domain. In an hour a client wants to browse your portfolio online.
right: Send the portfolio as a file

text: The online campaign goes live in the evening. At 9:05 p.m. you notice the link goes to a similarly named site — a plumbing store.
right: Fix the link on the fly

text: The site launches at midnight. At 11:30 p.m. the developer writes: “There’s one bug, but it’s funny.” The homepage is upside down.
In the evening you notice the client’s ad following you everywhere — social media, games, the weather app. Interest-based targeting nailed its creator.
In the evening the client wants a weekly report “with nice charts.” This week’s data: three clicks.
You made a selfie filter for the brand. In the evening it turns out it morphs faces into the client’s logo. Users love it; the client, less so.
In the evening the client finds a page called “Test_do_not_delete” where your designer left memes. It’s been indexed by search engines.
right: Joke that it’s a bonus feature

text: You set up push notifications for the client’s app. In the evening it turns out they hit every user every five minutes.
A blogger posted the integration without approval. In the evening the client watches him eat their product saying “eh, it’s okay.”
left: Ask him to take it down

text: The video hit a million views, but every comment is about the cat in the background. The cat wandered into the shot by accident.
In the evening you realize the client’s design system has 46 shades of grey. All are in use. Nobody remembers why.
In the evening you find the monthly campaign budget spent in three days. The platform “optimized delivery” at its own discretion.
At 10 p.m. the client writes that the site button is “too aggressive.” It’s pale blue and says “Learn more.”
In the evening someone posts a hundred identical negative reviews of the client’s product. All from one account. The client is panicking.
right: Calm the client with a call

text: In the evening the client gave the app beta to every employee. Now 800 people are sending you feedback.
right: Collect them in a sheet for later

text: Late in the evening the client wants music that plays when the site opens. You remember that being a thing twenty years ago.
left: Add it with a mute button

text: In the morning it turns out the podcast host read your ad spot word for word — including the note “pause here, smile.”
right: Play it up on the brand’s socials

text: The client spends half a day discussing an app icon the size of a fingernail. Eight people in the meeting each see something different, from a fox to a teapot.
The ad platform wants proof the client’s tea “really energizes,” or it won’t allow the word. The client has no such certificate.
In the evening the ad platform updated its interface. “Launch” is now “Begin the Journey.” You spend ten minutes finding where to start the campaign.
July, 32°C. The client wants a New Year’s campaign by Monday. The creatives, in shorts, try to “feel the winter magic.”
right: Brainstorm in a store’s cold room

text: A zoo ordered an ad. The star is a giraffe who refuses to look at the camera. The keeper says he’s “shy.”
A “Back to School” campaign for stationery. The client wants kids in the ad “thrilled about September.” Kids at the casting honestly say they’re not.
right: Ask the kids to act thrilled

text: A theater wants an ad for its premiere. The director wants the poster to “reveal nothing.” Not even the title.
right: Convince him to keep the title

text: A startup wants an ad but can’t explain what it does. At the meeting three founders give three different answers.
A family farm wants a milk ad “with real cows.” The shoot is at dawn in a field, in rubber boots you don’t own.
The client wants a spring campaign “full of freshness.” The shoot is in March: grimy snow and grey skies.
left: Shoot in a studio with flowers

text: The city library wants an ad “for young people.” Budget: two thousand and cookies for the team. The librarian is very sweet.
A developer wants the ad to feel “like Venice.” The complex sits by a highway, next to a duck pond.
A mobile carrier wants an ad about “coverage everywhere.” The shoot is in a forest where the crew has no signal. The producer can’t reach the driver.
Vacation season. Half the agency is away; the clients aren’t. Today you have four colleagues’ projects and one of your own.
A hockey club wants an ad for the season. The coach insists “nobody smiles — this is a serious sport.”
right: Sneak in one smile at the end

text: A charity asks for a free ad. The agency is fine with it, but you’d have to work weekends.
right: Chip away at it on weekdays

text: A contemporary art museum wants an exhibition ad. The curator won’t explain what it’s about: “Everyone will find their own meaning.”
The owner of a tiny shoe repair shop comes in with an envelope of cash. It’s enough for one business card.
left: Make a card and give advice

text: The circus director wants an elephant on the poster. There hasn’t been an elephant for ten years, but “people love elephants.”
left: Draw one with an honest caption

text: Shooting a fish-food ad. The fish won’t eat on camera and hide behind a rock. You are now the fish wrangler.
right: Wait as long as it takes

text: At the shoot, the bakery owner bakes bread for the shots himself and feeds the crew every ten minutes. An hour in, nobody can work.
left: Ask him to wait till after

text: The client approved the New Year’s ad in August. In November he wants it “more current”: snow is different this year.
A startup founder, heading into an investor meeting, asks you to “quickly sketch a logo on a napkin so there’s something to show.”
right: Refuse: logos aren’t born on napkins

text: A charity wants a campaign “without pity, but so people help.” Your team debates how not to slide into tearjerker.
A sports brand wants a real athlete in the ad. At the shoot he’s more exhausted than after a competition.
A jewelry brand wants a holiday ad where “every woman dreams of a ring.” The team thinks it’s an outdated take.
A toy brand wants the ad tested on kids. Five minutes in, the focus group of five children is dismantling the props.
A seaside restaurant wants a summer campaign. In the ad photo, a seagull snatches the burger right out of the model’s hand.
A startup pays the agency in shares. Today they’re worth lunch; tomorrow, who knows. The head asks your opinion.
A summer festival wants ads but can’t give dates, venue or lineup. “It’s all a surprise,” the organizers say.
At the car shoot the client forbids showing the car dirty, wet or moving. The ad is titled “No Limits.”
The client is launching a summer collection and wants a beach shoot. The budget covers a park by a fountain.
left: Shoot at the fountain with sand

text: A vet clinic wants staff pets in the ad. The owners demand “star” grooming.
A gym offers memberships as payment for the ad. You look at your schedule and know you’ll never go.
In the evening the client invites the agency to his holiday party and asks for “a little performance.” The agency has never performed.
The evening of December 30. The client writes: “Let’s launch the sale ad now, people are at home.” The team is off for the holidays.
After the show you advertised, the director takes a bow and thanks “the team who made the poster.” The audience applauds.
February 14. You spent all day on love-themed ads for a jewelry brand. In the evening you realize you forgot your own loved one.
right: Apologize and spend the evening together

text: In the evening the startup founder calls: “We pivoted. We’re not flower delivery anymore — we’re sock delivery.” The logo is a tulip.
You’re at the festival you promoted. The headliner is late, and the organizers ask you to “keep the crowd entertained somehow.”
An ice rink ordered a winter ad. In the evening your team is invited to “test the product.” You haven’t skated in fifteen years.
Your charity ad helped raise money. You’re invited to a thank-you dinner tonight, but you have a commercial deadline.
A summer evening, and the team suggests working on the office roof. Gorgeous sunset — but weak Wi-Fi and wind for the printouts.
In the evening the zoo sends thanks: after your ad the giraffe became a celebrity. He now has a fan club — and they want a second campaign.
At an evening fair where your client sells honey, he asks you to mind the stall “for half an hour” while he grabs food. Ninety minutes pass.
In the evening the small café you advertised sends a photo: there’s a queue outside. You spot a colleague in it.
In the evening you’re setting up a holiday installation at a mall. The 10,000-bulb garland won’t light. You need to find the one dead bulb.
You devised a social contest for the client. Three thousand entries arrive in the evening, and a winner is due by morning.
Opening night of the exhibition you advertised. The curator invites you to say a few words. You still don’t know what it’s about.
A vegetable warehouse wants ads “like fashion brands.” The shoot is between crates of cabbage, and the model in a coat is shivering.
A ski resort ordered an ad and invited the team for a weekend “for inspiration.” Nobody on the team can ski.
The owner of a Christmas tree lot wants ads for the last three days before the holiday. In the evening his “prepayment” arrives — a real tree at your door.
A wedding agency wants an ad about “eternal love.” In the evening the owners send edits — separately, because they’re divorcing.
A mannequin was left over from a shoot. Someone dresses it every morning and seats it at a free desk. Today it’s in your chair.
right: Move it to the meeting room

text: A designer put a sign on the restroom door — in the client’s brand style. The client arrives in an hour.
right: Leave it as an Easter egg

text: In the morning your monitor is covered in sticky notes reading “Bigger!” It’s the team’s joke after yesterday’s client review.
You notice the agency has misspelled its own name on its website for three years. Nobody noticed, including the head.
Every mug in the office kitchen bears a former client’s logo. Today’s client is drinking coffee from his main rival’s mug.
Your phone alarm accidentally plays the jingle you wrote for a client. You wake in a cold sweat.
right: Keep it, it wakes you up

text: Someone hung a moodboard in the agency elevator: “How Not to Make Ads.” Your work is in the middle.
The agency head accidentally sends the group chat a voice message meant for his cat. The voice is very tender.
right: Reply with a photo of your cat

text: The creative director declares “Brand Costume Day”: everyone dresses as one of their clients. You handle a dry-cleaning chain.
The agency printer has started adding a tiny cat at the end of every document. The sysadmin has no idea why. Today you print a bank contract.
The agency is strangely quiet this morning. Turns out everyone agreed on a “no-calls day” yesterday. Nobody told you, and you have five calls.
Someone ate your lunch from the agency fridge and left a note: “Delicious. Creativity demands sacrifice.”
right: Buy a lunchbox with a lock

text: This morning your desktop shows a wallpaper you didn’t set: the client’s giant logo. Colleagues act innocent.
The agency installed a “living wall” of plants for creativity. This morning half the team turns out to be allergic.
right: Keep it and hand out tissues

text: The client asks you not to mention his drink’s high sugar content: “Everyone knows anyway.” The law requires it.
A colleague tells you in confidence the client plans to leave for another agency. The head knows nothing.
The intern brings you coffee every morning, though you never asked. It’s awkward, but the coffee is great.
The client wants an ad that makes his competitor look foolish. No name, but everyone will recognize it.
Your agency’s new campaign looks a lot like a small studio’s work. The studio is already posting about it.
The creatives held a blind potluck. You taste something that resembles the client product you advertise.
Your jingle is stuck in the whole team’s heads. The account manager hums it during a meeting with a different client.
A blogger offers, for an extra fee, not to label the post as an ad. The client thinks that’s “more natural.”
A courier delivers a giant cake to the agency. Sender unknown; the icing says “Thanks for the edits.”
Someone turned a shoot prop into a coat rack. The prop is needed for tomorrow’s shoot, and it’s buried in jackets.
You’re offered a billboard spot where the ad for your favorite childhood ice cream used to hang. It’s no longer made.
right: Do a little homage to the ice cream

text: On set it turns out the whole crew, including you in a silly hat, is visible in the shop window reflection. The shot is perfect.
The client wants his employees dressed up as “satisfied customers” in the ad. He says everyone does it.
right: Film the staff, with a disclosure

text: Your new ergonomic chair arrived, but the creative director took it: “I need it more, I think harder.” Your back disagrees.
The agency bought a thousand pencils reading “Think Bolder.” They snap the first time you sharpen them.
left: Turn it into a case study

text: The client offers “a personal bonus” if the campaign skips some approvals with your management.
The creative director carries a rubber duck all day and tells it his ideas. He swears it helps. The duck is on your desk now.
left: Pitch the duck an idea too
right: Return the duck to its owner

text: You accidentally hit “Reply all” on a client email: “Okay, will do, though it’s weird.” Forty recipients.
In the evening the creative director leaves the rubber duck on your desk. You tell it about your day. It helps.
In the evening the client asks you to delete negative comments under the ad. They’re fair: the product really did break.
Leaving last, you see the agency’s neon “Be Bold” is half-lit: “Be B...” A TV crew comes tomorrow.
right: Joke about it in the interview

text: In the evening you find a note from the intern: “Thanks for not yelling when I deleted the project. I restored it.” You didn’t know he’d deleted it.
In the evening a courier delivers client samples to your home — seven boxes of baby diapers. You don’t have kids.
left: Give them to friends with babies
right: Take them to the office tomorrow

text: A colleague confesses he’s been passing off your “bigger logo” joke as his for three months. It became the agency meme.
In the evening you realize the client’s “9 out of 10 satisfied” stat comes from a survey of ten of his relatives.
right: Keep it, the client supplied it

text: In the empty office at night you hear odd sounds from the meeting room. It’s the robot vacuum, programmed by someone to sing the agency anthem.
right: Switch it off and go home

text: The client sends you personally an expensive gift “for your efforts.” Agency rules forbid gifts like that.
right: Put it in the team pool

text: In the evening the office next door is celebrating loudly. You knock — it’s another ad agency, celebrating winning your tender.
You’re offered a job at a rival agency — if you “bring your clients along.” They promise equity.
In the evening, looking through shoot photos, you realize the best shot was taken by the intern on his phone.
In the evening you see an ad-industry meme online: “When the client asks for a bigger logo.” The picture is your photo from a shoot.
right: Ask for it to be removed

text: The agency issued new badges with “creative job titles.” Yours says “Lord of Deadlines.” Today you meet a very serious bank.
The agency is voting on a meeting room name. Your “One More Edit” is leading, but the head wants “something inspiring.”
Leaving in the evening, you find your bike covered in client-logo stickers. Done neatly, and even beautifully.
left: Keep it as an art piece

text: In the evening you accidentally empty the shared drive’s trash. Five minutes later someone asks in chat: “Has anyone seen my file? I deleted it temporarily.”
Late at night you’re drawing at home, just for yourself. An hour in you realize it’s the client’s logo again. Your hand did it.
right: Send the sketch to the client

text: Friday morning. Just one meeting on the calendar, at 5 p.m. Suspiciously calm. The account manager is already heading over with a laptop.
A freelance animator delivers early, error-free, apologizing that it’s “only a day early.” You can’t believe your eyes.
You decided to start each day with ten minutes of drawing “for yourself.” Today ten became forty, and you’re late for stand-up.
The client calls just to say thanks for the campaign. No edits, no “but.” You wait for the catch the whole call.
In the morning the agency head offers you time off himself: “You look worn out.” You didn’t know it showed.
At the morning brainstorm, for the first time in a month, nobody is on their phone. Ideas are flowing. The creative director suggests an extra hour.
The account manager brings you coffee and says: “I get why you were mad. No more promising ‘by morning.’” You’re touched.
A morning email: your little library campaign won the top prize at a public service ad festival.
The designer who “burned out on blue” a month ago is back from vacation and asks for the bluest project. Says he missed it.
right: Give him something in another color

text: You wake up without an alarm, rested for the first time in a month. It’s 9:40. Stand-up is at 10.
The intern shows you his first solo work. It’s good. And you can see what he learned from you.
In the morning you notice someone fixed the coffee machine, replaced the lamps and removed the mannequin. The office suddenly feels grown up.
left: Find the hero and say thanks

text: The client writes: “The logo can be smaller. I realize you were right.” You print the email and hang it over your desk.
For the first time you made a weekly plan with lunch breaks, work-free evenings and weekends. It reads like science fiction.
The freelancer who once vanished with the files writes: “Sorry. I’m back. Here are the files. And 50% off.”
The creative director gathers everyone and announces a “week without late-night edits.” The creatives applaud; the account managers exchange nervous looks.
right: Ask for rules for account managers

text: Friday lunchtime. The client approves the campaign on the first go. The team has no idea what to do with the rest of the day.
A talented freelancer asks to join the staff. Her work is great, but she frankly says she hates meetings.
At the meeting the client says: “Do what you think is right. We trust you.” First time in five years.
For the first time in a month you’re eating lunch in the park instead of at your desk. Phone in your backpack. Pigeons eye your sandwich.
The media buyer says the campaign had the best results of the year. The client wants “the same, again.” The creatives want something new.
The team asks you to run a “year in review”: what worked, what didn’t. Someone already wrote “Bigger logo” under “Didn’t work.”
The producer admits he came in under budget on the last shoot and wants to refund the client. The agency head wants to keep it “for development.”
The art director and the account manager, who argued all year, come to you together with a joint idea. It’s excellent.
The agency head proposes a four-day week — “trial for a month.” He asks you to draft the plan.
A client you’ve worked with for five years is retiring. At the farewell meeting he says your ideas were the best part of his career.
For the first time this year you came up with an idea not for a brief, but just because, on a walk. It suits no client.
right: Pitch it as an agency project

text: The intern got a full-time offer. He asks whether to accept, or “quit for pastry school while there’s still time.”
right: Tell him to follow his heart

text: The agency lawyer, who always struck everything out, proposes a bold slogan wording himself. Everyone’s stunned.
For the first time accounts pays bonuses on time, unprompted. The email is titled “No Catch.” The team still searches for the catch.
Your former mentor messages: he saw your latest work and is proud. He never praised anyone.
Friday, 6 p.m. Inbox empty. Chats silent. You could leave on time for the first time in six months, but “what if” keeps nagging.
In the evening the team celebrates the end of the season. Everyone shares the year’s weirdest edit. The winner gets a trophy shaped like a giant logo.
You get home on time. Your family eyes you suspiciously: “Did you get fired?” You laugh — no, it’s just that kind of day.
In the evening the creative director stops by: “You know, this year would’ve been duller without you.” And leaves before you can answer.
In the evening, updating your portfolio, you realize you did more this year than you thought. Even a few pieces you’re proud of.
In the evening the client sends a voice note: “I want you doing our ads next year. All of them. Logo can be bigger.” You can hear him smiling.
right: Ask to keep the logo as is

text: Friday evening. You decide to mute work chats until Monday. Your finger hovers over the button.
The freelancer you worked with all year sends a card: your team drawn as superheroes. Your superpower: “approves on first try.”
In the evening the agency head asks everyone for one word about the year. Most write “edits.” You write…
Your cat sits on the laptop again. This time you don’t shoo him — you close the lid and go to bed.
right: Move the cat and finish up

text: Your last evening before vacation. You write the auto-reply: “I’m on vacation. The logo can be made bigger without me.”
Your desk neighbor heads home leaving a note: “Thanks for being there this year. Even when the render crashed.”
You dream you’re on an awards stage and a client shouts from the audience, “Make the logo bigger!” Everyone laughs, you too.
right: Write the dream down as an idea

text: In the evening you pack for vacation. Your hand reaches for the laptop “just in case.”
Friday evening. You leave the agency, and the neon “Be Bold” sign is finally fully lit. A good omen.
In the evening you tally up: no edits after 10 p.m. this week, two free evenings and one idea the client accepted immediately.
A new client says at the first meeting: “We’ve read about you. They say you push back on clients when it matters. That’s what we need.”
In the evening you pass your first billboard, still up after five years. Honestly, the logo on it is a bit small.
right: Snap a photo for the client

text: Friends invite you to dinner on Friday night. For the first time this year you can say yes with no caveats.
